papers.abstract: Ex-ante models can now predict how much energy a public electric-vehicle charging site will sell before it is built. A distribution network development plan (DNDP), however, is not denominated in kilowatt-hours per month; it is denominated in kilowatts at a named transformer, at the hour the network peaks. This paper supplies the missing translation layer and demonstrates it on a full-scale utility dataset: 101,020 revenue-grade charging sessions from 328 public stations, joined to the measured loading of 41,128 distribution transformers across West Java, Indonesia. Three results follow. First, public fast charging is not an off-peak load: reconstructed at 15-minute resolution, the aggregate charging curve retains 88–91% of its daily maximum throughout the 18:00–22:00 evening peak window, and 20.4% of monthly energy is delivered in those four hours against 16.7% under a flat profile. Second, the relationship between forecast energy and design peak is strongly sub-linear, P = 0.133·E^0.695 (R² = 0.810), so the nameplate-times-coincidence rule that dominates connection studies over-estimates 74% of sites and carries 1.7 times the error of an energy-based rule. Third, inverting the transfer function prices network headroom in the same unit as the demand forecast: the 41,128 transformers can host 452 GWh/month of charging in aggregate, roughly twenty times the 2030 provincial requirement, yet under a demand-led rollout 49% of the transformers that host charging today would exceed 100% loading, and the 13% of 2 km cells in deficit contain 46% of the forecast energy. Reallocating half of the increment under the statutory coverage obligation removes the violation entirely. Charging demand in this network is therefore not a capacity problem but an allocation problem, and the coverage mandate is a network-relief instrument rather than a network cost.

papers.html:
Tailpipe to Smokestack: Marginal Emission Factors and the Illusion of Zero-Emission Mobility on a Coal-Dominated Grid

Qashtalani Haramaini

Monash University Indonesia, Jakarta, Indonesia

Abstract

Electric vehicles are credited with zero tailpipe emissions, and national decarbonisation targets are built on that premise. This paper argues that in a coal-dominated archipelagic power system the result is determined not by the fleet-average grid emission factor but by two distributional tails that conventional accounting removes. The merit-order tail concerns supply: the marginal kilowatt-hour serving new charging load is set by the dispatchable stack, and because public charging is empirically midday-weighted rather than evening-peaked, that margin is mid-merit coal rather than gas peaking plant. The infrastructure tail concerns demand: public charging utilisation is heavy-tailed, so the embodied carbon of a large population of near-idle chargers is amortised over very little delivered energy.

We integrate 528 georeferenced generating units (87.4 GW) across Indonesia’s eight interconnected systems, 3,201 georeferenced public charging stations (4,997 chargers, 121.6 MW), and 101,020 metered charging sessions. Station-level energy is extremely unequal (Gini 0.769; the least-utilised half of stations delivers 2.6% of energy), and the operator’s own national classification places 2,193 stations in the low-utilisation class with none in the medium or high classes. Amortised infrastructure carbon ranges from 4 to 749 g CO2 per delivered kWh between the 10th and 90th percentile station. Combining both tails, a battery electric vehicle charged at a 90th-percentile station emits 281–318 g CO2/km well-to-wheel, 1.56–1.76 times a conventional benchmark.

We introduce two metrics. The carbon-breakeven utilisation A* is the minimum annual throughput at which a charger is carbon-justified against the vehicle it displaces; it is 6,418 kWh/yr in Jamali, 26,439 kWh/yr in Kalimantan, and undefined in Sulawesi and Maluku, where no level of utilisation suffices. The Compound Tail Index ranks systems by the combined penalty. We show the two tails are spatially coincident, so equity-driven deployment and carbon minimisation are, under present conditions, in direct conflict.

1. Introduction

The decarbonisation case for electric vehicles rests on a substitution argument: combustion emissions at the tailpipe are replaced by generation emissions at the power plant, and the latter fall over time as the generation mix cleans up. In systems where that mix is already low-carbon the argument is robust to accounting detail. In systems where it is not, the conclusion becomes acutely sensitive to two choices that are usually made implicitly: which kilowatt-hour is assumed to serve the charging load, and whether the carbon embodied in the charging infrastructure sits inside or outside the boundary.

Indonesia is a demanding test case on both counts. Coal supplies 61.2% of the georeferenced capacity examined here; fossil capacity exceeds 73% in every interconnected system and reaches 100% in Maluku. At the same time the public charging network has expanded rapidly ahead of vehicle uptake, producing a large population of assets with very low throughput. Policy evaluation to date has largely used a national or system-average grid emission factor and has treated charging infrastructure as carbon-free once installed. Both simplifications, we argue, delete precisely the terms that determine the answer.

This paper makes those terms explicit and quantifies them from observed data rather than assumption.

2. Novelty and Contributions

The contribution is not a new emission-factor estimator nor a new siting algorithm. It is the joint treatment of the supply tail and the demand tail at the vehicle level, using measured utilisation, and the two decision metrics that fall out of it. Six specific claims to novelty are made.

N1 — Integrated supply–demand carbon accounting across all eight Indonesian interconnected systems. Existing work treats generation mix and charging infrastructure in separate literatures. We join a georeferenced generation inventory, a georeferenced national charging asset register, and session-level metering into a single spatial frame, which is what makes the coincidence of the two tails observable at all.

N2 — The infrastructure tail is measured, not assumed. Charger life-cycle studies conventionally assume a constant utilisation. We derive the full empirical distribution of station throughput from 101,020 metered sessions and carry it through as a distribution. Because infrastructure carbon intensity is a ratio whose denominator is heavy-tailed, its mean is uninformative; the upper percentiles carry the result, and only a measured distribution exposes them.

N3 — A new decision metric: the carbon-breakeven utilisation A*. We invert the accounting to ask what minimum annual throughput makes a charger carbon-justified against the vehicle it displaces. This converts an abstract life-cycle result into a commissioning threshold a planner can apply to a specific site. Its corollary is stronger still: in systems whose marginal factor already exceeds the displaced-vehicle benchmark, A* is undefined, and no level of utilisation redeems the asset.

N4 — A new ranking metric: the Compound Tail Index, which expresses the tail-station well-to-wheel intensity relative to the displaced conventional vehicle, allowing systems to be ordered by the combined penalty rather than by grid factor alone.

N5 — An empirical finding that determines which margin applies. Public direct-current charging in the metered province is midday-weighted and close to flat (37.2% of energy between 09:00 and 15:00 against 30.8% between 17:00 and 22:00), not evening-peaked as residential charging models assume. It therefore sits on the mid-merit coal margin rather than the gas and diesel peaking margin. We report the margin as a band bounded by these two cases and show the choice moves the result by roughly 30 g CO2/km.

N6 — Spatial evidence of an equity–carbon conflict. We show that the systems with the highest marginal emission factors host the fewest charging assets and therefore the thinnest demand per asset, so equitable geographic deployment moves the network toward both tails simultaneously. This is stated here as a measured spatial relationship rather than a conjecture.

3. Data

Three sources are combined. All are static snapshots. No confidential operational data and no personally identifying attributes are used.

3.1 Generation fleet

A georeferenced inventory of 528 generating units totalling 87,361 MW, assembled from the national electricity supply business plan and cross-matched to open geographic sources. Each record carries coordinates, technology class, nameplate capacity, operating status, and system membership. The inventory also contains 502 transmission substations and 2,357 transmission line segments, used to confirm system membership and to provide the network skeleton in the maps that follow. Coal-fired capacity is 53,452 MW.

3.2 Public charging assets

A national register of 3,212 public charging stations with coordinates, rated power, charger and connector counts, operator category and operational status. Of these, 3,201 fall inside the eight system envelopes and are retained, comprising 4,997 chargers and 121.6 MW of installed charging capacity. Two auxiliary registers are used: an operator utilisation classification covering 2,193 stations, and a register of 1,207 chargers recorded as inactive.

3.3 Metered charging sessions

A complete month of session-level records for one province: 101,020 sessions, 2,259,548 kWh, 329 stations, with timestamp to the second, energy, duration, connector rating and station identifier. Median session energy is 19.8 kWh over a median 0.68 hours. This province is the most mature charging market in the country, a fact exploited in Section 4.5.

[gambar: image1.png]

Figure 1. Spatial coincidence of generation and charging assets. Marker area scales with the square root of installed capacity; transmission lines provide the network skeleton. Charging stations concentrate on Java, where coal capacity is also densest; the eastern systems combine near-total fossil dependence with almost no charging demand.

4. Method

4.1 System assignment

Each generating unit and each charging station is assigned to one of the eight interconnected systems by coordinate envelope. Eleven stations fall outside all envelopes and are dropped. Assignment is verified against the operator’s administrative unit coding.

4.2 Emission factors and the margin band

Two factors are computed per system from the capacity inventory. The generation-weighted average factor AEF weights each technology by capacity multiplied by an assumed capacity factor and by its direct emission factor at the busbar. The dispatchable-margin factor MEF restricts the weighting to the thermal set of coal, combined cycle, open cycle gas, diesel and gas engine capacity, reflecting that hydro, geothermal and the very small solar fleet are either baseload-committed or non-dispatchable and therefore do not set the margin.

Because the identity of the marginal unit depends on where in the load duration curve the charging load falls, we report a band rather than a point. The lower bound is a peaking margin, computed over diesel, gas engine and open-cycle capacity only; the upper bound is a coal margin. The measured charging profile determines which end of the band is relevant, and Section 5.2 shows that it is the coal end. Both factors are referred to the vehicle inlet by network losses of 8.5% and charger efficiency of 0.92. Technology parameters are held fixed across systems so that all inter-system variation is driven by observed fleet composition.

4.3 The infrastructure tail

For each station, monthly metered energy is annualised. The empirical Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient of annual station energy characterise the tail. Embodied carbon is modelled as a hardware term proportional to rated power, taken as 40 kg CO2e per kW, plus a fixed site term of 8 t CO2e covering civil works and the medium-voltage connection. Over an assumed asset life of ten years, the infrastructure carbon intensity of delivered energy is the embodied total divided by lifetime delivered energy. The distribution of this quantity, not its mean, is the object of interest.

4.4 Carbon-breakeven utilisation and the Compound Tail Index

Let the displaced vehicle emit a benchmark intensity per kilometre and let specific consumption be 0.17 kWh/km. Setting the electric vehicle’s well-to-wheel intensity equal to that benchmark defines a maximum admissible infrastructure carbon intensity, and inverting the amortisation gives the carbon-breakeven utilisation A*: the minimum annual throughput at which the charger is carbon-justified. Where the marginal factor alone already exceeds the benchmark, the admissible infrastructure intensity is negative and A* is undefined. The Compound Tail Index is the ratio of the well-to-wheel intensity at the 90th-percentile station to the conventional benchmark, so that values above one identify systems in which a tail-station vehicle is worse than the technology it displaces.

4.5 Transfer to systems without metering

Session-level metering exists for one province only. We transfer the shape of the utilisation distribution, not its level, to the remaining systems. This is deliberately conservative: the metered province has the highest vehicle registration density in the country, so applying its distribution elsewhere over-states utilisation and therefore under-states infrastructure carbon intensity in every other system. Compound penalties reported outside that province are consequently lower bounds. The operator’s national tagging supports this direction, placing 2,193 stations in the low-utilisation class and none above it.

Centre: the measured station throughput distribution, whose lower half delivers 2.6% of energy. Right: the resulting well-to-wheel intensity as each term is admitted to the accounting boundary.

5. Results

5.1 Both tails are steep

Station-level energy is extremely unequal. The Gini coefficient of annualised station throughput is 0.769; the ten busiest stations deliver 28.3% of energy while the least-utilised half of the network delivers 2.6%. The operator’s own national classification is more striking still: the medium and high utilisation classes are empty, so the infrastructure tail is not a property of a few outliers but the central feature of the deployment. Amortised over delivered energy, embodied carbon contributes 4 g CO2/kWh at the 10th percentile station, 81 g CO2/kWh at the median, and 749 g CO2/kWh at the 90th percentile. The upper-tail figure is of the same order as the generation intensity itself: for a tail station the charger, not the power plant, is the larger emitter per unit of energy delivered.

[gambar: image3.png]

Figure 3. The infrastructure tail. (a) Lorenz curve of annualised station energy from 101,020 metered sessions. (b) Operator utilisation classification of the national network, in which the medium and high classes are empty.

5.2 The charging load does not fall on the evening peak

The diurnal distribution of delivered energy is close to flat, with 37.2% of energy delivered between 09:00 and 15:00 and 30.8% between 17:00 and 22:00. Public direct-current charging therefore behaves quite differently from residential charging, and the common assumption that electric vehicle load aggravates the evening peak does not hold for this segment. The consequence for the accounting is direct: load added in the middle of the day is not served by gas and diesel peaking plant at the top of the stack but by mid-merit coal. The peaking margin computed for these systems lies between 0.57 and 0.67 kg CO2/kWh, below the coal margin of 0.95, so treating the margin as peaking would understate the result by roughly 30 g CO2/km. The measured profile is what rules that case out.

[gambar: image4.png]

Figure 4. Diurnal distribution of delivered energy across 101,020 sessions. The dashed line is a uniform profile; the shaded band marks the solar generation window.

5.3 System characteristics and spatial coincidence

Fossil capacity exceeds 73% in every system and reaches 100% in Maluku. Charging assets are strongly concentrated: Jamali holds 71.4% of stations and 77.4% of chargers, while the four eastern systems together hold 4.7% of stations. The relationship between marginal emission factor and installed chargers is inverse and steep, so the systems with the dirtiest margin host the thinnest demand per asset. The two tails fall in the same places.

5.5 The carbon-breakeven utilisation

The breakeven threshold varies by an order of magnitude across systems and becomes undefined in two of them. In Jamali a 50 kW unit must deliver at least 6,418 kWh per year to be carbon-justified against a conventional vehicle; 63.8% of observed stations meet that threshold. The same inversion applied to the grid rather than the charger yields a second threshold. For an electric vehicle to beat a conventional vehicle the busbar factor must fall below 0.891 kg CO2/kWh; to beat an efficient hybrid it must fall below 0.654 kg CO2/kWh. Only Sumatra, at 0.651, is currently near the latter. This is the sharpest form of the paper’s claim: at present grid intensities the electric vehicle in Indonesia is competitive with the conventional vehicle it usually displaces, but not with the hybrid it could displace instead.

6. Discussion

6.1 The equity–carbon conflict

Charging infrastructure is currently concentrated where vehicles are, which is also where the grid is comparatively least carbon-intensive. Spatial equity arguments, and the universal-service obligation that follows from them, push deployment toward the eastern systems. Figure 5 shows that this movement is toward higher marginal emission factors and, because vehicle density there is lower still, toward deeper infrastructure tails. Under present conditions equity-driven deployment and carbon minimisation are in direct conflict. This does not argue against equitable deployment. It argues that the carbon claim should not be attached to it, and that the two objectives require separate instruments and separate reporting.

6.2 Where the binding term is

The decomposition identifies which lever acts on which term. Adding stations acts on neither: it lengthens the infrastructure tail without changing the margin. Raising utilisation acts directly on infrastructure carbon intensity, and the elasticity is largest exactly where the problem is worst, because that intensity is inversely proportional to throughput. Redeploying the 1,207 chargers currently recorded as inactive to demonstrated-demand sites converts stranded embodied carbon into delivered energy at no additional manufacturing burden. Changing the generation margin acts on the other term but on a much longer timescale.

6.3 The midday window

The observed profile is the one constructive finding. Because public fast charging is midday-weighted rather than evening-peaked, a substantial share of it already coincides with the solar generation window. Solar capacity is presently negligible in all eight systems, below 2.3% everywhere and below 0.1% in Sumatra and Maluku, so this coincidence is unexploited. Co-locating distributed solar with high-throughput stations addresses the supply tail at the point where the demand tail is thinnest, and is the only lever identified here that improves both terms simultaneously.

6.4 Policy implications

Utilisation floors should precede station-count targets. A* provides the threshold in physical units, and it is system-specific rather than national.

Procurement and reporting should be expressed as carbon per delivered kilowatt-hour rather than stations installed, which makes the infrastructure term visible to the decision-maker.

Emission reporting for electric mobility should state which factor is used. The difference between the average and tail boundaries in Table 3 is larger than the difference between an electric and a conventional vehicle.

In systems where A* is undefined, network expansion should be sequenced behind generation replacement rather than run in parallel with it.

7. Limitations

Emission factors are derived from capacity composition with fixed technology parameters rather than from metered dispatch, which is not publicly available; they should be read as structural indicators rather than settled values, and calibration against official system factors is the natural next step. The margin is approximated by capacity-weighted subsets of the dispatchable fleet, which is appropriate for systems with negligible variable renewable capacity but would require unit-commitment data to refine. Embodied carbon coefficients are literature-order estimates and the 90th-percentile result scales linearly in them; the qualitative conclusion holds for any coefficient above roughly one third of the values used. Session metering covers one province and one month, so seasonality is not captured, and the shape transfer of Section 4.5 is an assumption, albeit a conservative one. Finally, 1,013 stations operated by third parties report no telemetry, so measured utilisation reflects the operator-owned subset; if third-party stations are less utilised, the tail is deeper than reported.

8. Conclusion

Evaluating electric mobility in a coal-dominated archipelagic system at a fleet-average grid factor, with charging infrastructure treated as carbon-free, systematically flatters the result. Once the merit-order tail and the infrastructure tail are both admitted, the well-to-wheel intensity of an electric vehicle charged at a 90th-percentile station reaches 281–318 g CO2/km, between 1.56 and 1.76 times a conventional benchmark, and the two tails are shown to fall in the same places. The carbon-breakeven utilisation converts that finding into a commissioning threshold, and shows that in two of the eight systems no threshold exists. The policy consequence is that utilisation, not station count, is the carbon-relevant variable, and that the midday concentration of public charging is an unexploited opportunity to attack both tails at once.

papers.abstract: Electric vehicles are credited with zero tailpipe emissions, and national decarbonisation targets are built on that premise. This paper argues that in a coal-dominated archipelagic power system the result is determined not by the fleet-average grid emission factor but by two distributional tails that conventional accounting removes. The merit-order tail concerns supply: the marginal kilowatt-hour serving new charging load is set by the dispatchable stack, and because public charging is empirically midday-weighted rather than evening-peaked, that margin is mid-merit coal rather than gas peaking plant. The infrastructure tail concerns demand: public charging utilisation is heavy-tailed, so the embodied carbon of a large population of near-idle chargers is amortised over very little delivered energy. We integrate 528 georeferenced generating units (87.4 GW) across Indonesia’s eight interconnected systems, 3,201 georeferenced public charging stations (4,997 chargers, 121.6 MW), and 101,020 metered charging sessions. Station-level energy is extremely unequal (Gini 0.769; the least-utilised half of stations delivers 2.6% of energy), and the operator’s own national classification places 2,193 stations in the low-utilisation class with none in the medium or high classes. Amortised infrastructure carbon ranges from 4 to 749 g CO2 per delivered kWh between the 10th and 90th percentile station. Combining both tails, a battery electric vehicle charged at a 90th-percentile station emits 281–318 g CO2/km well-to-wheel, 1.56–1.76 times a conventional benchmark. We introduce two metrics. The carbon-breakeven utilisation A* is the minimum annual throughput at which a charger is carbon-justified against the vehicle it displaces; it is 6,418 kWh/yr in Jamali, 26,439 kWh/yr in Kalimantan, and undefined in Sulawesi and Maluku, where no level of utilisation suffices. The Compound Tail Index ranks systems by the combined penalty. We show the two tails are spatially coincident, so equity-driven deployment and carbon minimisation are, under present conditions, in direct conflict.

papers.html:
Captive Generation And The Verification-Incentive Inversion: Spatially Differentiated Grid Emission Factors And Cbam Exposure Of Indonesia'S Export Industry

Haramaini, Q.1

1Monash University Indonesia, Jakarta, Indonesia

qashtalani.haramaini@monash.edu

Abstract

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) entered its definitive regime on 1 January 2026, pricing the indirect emissions embedded in electricity used to produce imported aluminium, steel, cement and fertilisers. Exporters may either accept a country-level default value or verify an installation-specific actual value. This study shows that where national carbon intensity is spatially bimodal, that binary choice inverts the incentive it was designed to create. We compile a georeferenced inventory of 526 generating units (95.4 GW) and 933 transmission substations across Indonesia's eight interconnected systems, separate grid-connected from captive industrial self-generation using an auditable registry, and estimate zonal emission factors with Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation. Captive units hold 17.7 % of capacity but 27.6 % of generation-side CO2. Including them raises the Sulawesi emission factor by 38 %, Papua by 40 % and Maluku by 27 %, while leaving Java–Bali unchanged; provincial factors span a 3.1-fold range. At EUR 75.36/tCO2 the indirect charge on unwrought aluminium varies by EUR 324 per tonne between zones. Producers in five of eight zones, covering the entire nickel-processing captive belt, would pay more by verifying than by accepting the default.

Keywords: carbon border adjustment mechanism; grid emission factor; captive power; embedded emissions; Indonesia

1. INTRODUCTION

The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) completed its reporting-only transitional phase on 31 December 2025 and entered its definitive regime on 1 January 2026. Importers of cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity above a 50-tonne annual threshold must now hold authorised declarant status and surrender certificates against the verified embedded emissions of their goods (European Union, 2023). The European Commission published the first quarterly certificate price on 7 April 2026 at EUR 75.36 per tonne of CO2.

Embedded emissions under CBAM comprise direct process emissions and indirect emissions from electricity consumed in production (European Commission, 2025a). For electro-intensive goods the indirect term dominates: primary aluminium consumes roughly 14 MWh per tonne of metal, so the carbon intensity of the electricity supply, rather than the smelter process, sets the liability. A national inventory statistic has therefore become a determinant of trade competitiveness.

Indonesia is exposed on two fronts. Its CBAM-covered export basket is growing, and the electricity supplying that industry has an unusual structure. A rapidly expanding fleet of captive coal plants, built inside industrial parks and connected to no public grid, now supplies most of the electricity consumed by the metal-processing export sector. Operating captive capacity reached 25.9 GW in 2024, over three quarters coal-fired, with Sulawesi (10.5 GW) and Maluku (4.5 GW) the largest concentrations (JETP Indonesia Secretariat, 2025), emitting an estimated 131 MtCO2, roughly 37 % of power-sector emissions (IESR, 2026). Coal-powered Indonesian nickel producers report 57–70 tCO2 per tonne of nickel against 28.7 for the single producer supplied by its own hydroelectric cascade (Peh, 2024).

Carbon accounting practice does not see this fleet. Indonesian emission factors are published per interconnected system by the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (MEMR, 2021) and derive from the dispatch of utilities and independent power producers serving the public grid; off-grid self-generation lies outside the boundary. The same fleet sits outside the intensity-based emissions trading scheme applied to grid-connected coal plants (Climate Action Tracker, 2026), so no domestic carbon price attaches to it and none can be deducted from a CBAM liability.

Three literatures bear on this problem and none closes it. Work on electricity emission factors is methodologically mature but has been applied to systems with complete metered dispatch and no significant off-grid segment (Ryan et al., 2016; Tranberg et al., 2019). Assessments of border carbon adjustment incidence use computable general equilibrium models resolved at country and sector level, treating national emission intensity as an exogenous scalar (Böhringer et al., 2022; Perdana & Vielle, 2022). Studies of Indonesian captive coal document its growth but stop at description. This study connects them, and asks whether a country-level default value can function as intended when the underlying distribution of carbon intensity is bimodal. The question is regionally relevant: captive industrial power is expanding across several ASEAN member states, and the answer bears directly on how APAEC 2026–2030 should treat sub-national energy data.

2. METHODOLOGY

2.1 Data and Captive Classification

The dataset covers Indonesia's eight interconnected systems (Jamali, Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Maluku, NTB, NTT, Papua) in three georeferenced layers: 933 transmission substations with coordinates, voltage class, transformer count, capacity in MVA and province, extracted from the supply-side tables of the 2025–2034 electricity supply business plan (PLN, 2025) and matched to OpenStreetMap geometry by fuzzy name matching; 526 operating generating units with coordinates, technology class, installed capacity, province and operator, obtained by Overpass extraction from OpenStreetMap and cross-checked against the same plan;. Fifty-six small units lacking a capacity attribute are imputed at the median of their technology class within their system and contribute under 1 % of national capacity.

No source attribute marks self-generation, so units are classified through an explicit registry: a unit is captive if its name or operator tag identifies an industrial host (smelter, alumina refinery, pulp and paper mill, cement plant, chemical works, mine) or a dedicated industrial-estate licensee. The registry is conservative, capturing 17.0 GW against the 25.9 GW reported for 2024, so the biases reported below are lower bounds, and it is technology-neutral, admitting the 365 MW Larona–Balambano–Karebbe hydroelectric cascade operated by a nickel producer.

2.2 Zonal Emission Factor Estimator

For a zone z under accounting boundary b (grid, captive, or system-wide), the emission factor is the generation-weighted mean of technology emission factors, where each unit contributes installed capacity multiplied by its capacity factor, 8760 hours, and its operating emission factor. Capacity factors and emission factors are treated as random variables with triangular distributions, and the estimator is evaluated over 20,000 Monte Carlo draws, giving a mean and a 5th–95th percentile interval for every zone and boundary. Emission factors combine IPCC default fuel factors with representative net thermal efficiencies for the Indonesian fleet (IPCC, 2006). Captive units receive a separate, higher capacity-factor distribution, since a plant sized to a continuous metallurgical load runs at a higher duty cycle than one dispatched against a diurnal demand curve.

2.3 CBAM Exposure and Verification Incentive

The indirect liability for a CBAM good is its specific electricity consumption multiplied by the zonal emission factor and the certificate price, taken as EUR 75.36. An installation reports actual values only if doing so lowers its liability, that is if its specific consumption times its zonal emission factor is below the country default value carrying the applicable mark-up. Default values are set above the producer-country average and carry mark-ups of 10 % in 2026, 20 % in 2027 and 30 % from 2028 (European Commission, 2025b). The mark-up is the instrument by which the Regulation intends to make verification worthwhile. We evaluate the condition with the default set equal to the national system-wide factor estimated here, which is the assumption most favourable to that logic.

3. RESULT AND DISCUSSION

3.1 Spatial Structure of the Fleet

The inventory covers 95.4 GW across 526 units. Figure 1 shows two structural features. Grid generation concentrates along the Java–Bali corridor and the Sumatran spine, co-located with dense substation coverage. Captive units appear as isolated points of very large unit capacity in eastern Indonesia, in locations with almost no surrounding substation infrastructure, which is the spatial signature of an industrial enclave supplying itself. Captive capacity totals 17.0 GW, or 17.7 % of mapped capacity, but 22.2 % of estimated generation and 27.6 % of estimated CO2. Four units, Weda Bay (4.0 GW), Labota (3.4 GW), IMIP Morowali (2.1 GW) and Delong Nickel Phase II (1.8 GW), account for 66 % of captive capacity and all serve nickel processing.

3.2 Zonal Emission Factors

Table 1 reports the central result. Under the grid-only boundary the eight systems span 0.60–0.90 tCO2/MWh; under the system-wide boundary they span 0.66–0.96. The change is highly uneven. Jamali, Kalimantan and NTT move by under one percent because their captive fleets are small relative to a large public grid. Sulawesi rises by 38 %, Papua by 40 % and Maluku by 27 %.

The mechanism is visible in the energy shares. In Maluku, captive units supply an estimated 98.0 % of system generation; in Sulawesi 80.2 %; in Papua 63.4 %. In these zones the public grid is not the dominant electricity system, and a factor derived from it describes a minority of the electrons actually consumed. Sulawesi is the sharpest case: its public grid, carrying substantial hydro and geothermal, is among the cleanest in Indonesia at 0.64 tCO2/MWh, while the zone as a whole is among the dirtiest at 0.89. Resolving to province widens the spread to a factor of 3.1, from 0.31 tCO2/MWh in North Sumatra to 0.96 in North Maluku. At national level the boundary choice moves the factor from 0.688 to 0.738, an increase of 7.3 %. That the aggregate effect is modest is precisely why the distributional effect escapes national reporting.

3.3 CBAM Exposure and the Verification-Incentive Inversion

For unwrought aluminium the indirect charge ranges from EUR 692 per tonne in Sumatra to EUR 1015 in Maluku at the central certificate price, a spread of EUR 324 per tonne attributable solely to the location of the electricity supply. Within Sulawesi alone the boundary choice alone is worth EUR 259 per tonne.

Table 2 and Figure 2 evaluate the verification condition. Setting the default equal to the national system-wide factor with the 2026 mark-up gives a default liability of EUR 857 per tonne. Five of eight zones carry actual liabilities above that threshold, so an installation in any of them lowers its CBAM bill by declining to verify: the saving is EUR 158 per tonne in Maluku, EUR 92 in Kalimantan and EUR 76 in Sulawesi. Producers in Sumatra, Jamali and NTT face the opposite position and gain EUR 165, EUR 124 and EUR 40 per tonne respectively by verifying.

Raising the mark-up to its 2028 level of 30 % moves the threshold to EUR 1015 per tonne, lifting every zone except Maluku above the break-even line. The phase-in therefore does eventually restore the intended incentive, but only after the affected zones have had three compliance years in which the cheapest strategy was opacity.

The result is not an artefact of the modelled default. It follows from the shape of the distribution. A default constructed as a country average plus a mark-up separates cleanly into verifying and non-verifying populations only if the underlying distribution is unimodal and the mark-up exceeds its upper dispersion. The Indonesian distribution is bimodal, with a grid mode near 0.62–0.69 and a captive-coal mode near 0.95, and the gap between the modes is 45 % of the lower one, larger than any mark-up scheduled before 2028. Under those conditions the country default functions as a transfer to the high-intensity mode financed by the low-intensity mode, and the transparency incentive operates in reverse precisely where transparency matters most.

3.4 Policy Implications

Three implications follow. First, aggregation is a trade cost: an exporter in Central Sulawesi asserting the national factor asserts a number 29 % below its own supply, while producers in North Sumatra are penalised by a national average more than twice their actual intensity. Second, emissions excluded from the domestic scheme are undeductible: the 27.6 % of power-sector CO2 attributed to captive units attracts no domestic carbon price and therefore generates no CBAM deduction. Extending allowance allocation to captive plants under the framework introduced by Presidential Regulation 110/2025 would convert part of that flow into domestic revenue while creating the abatement signal the current design lacks. Third, the provincial results suggest a siting strategy: North Sumatra, Jakarta, West Java, North Sulawesi and Lampung all sit below 0.51 tCO2/MWh and are served by dense substation infrastructure, so locating new electro-intensive export capacity on these nodes rather than replicating the captive-coal enclave model would cut CBAM exposure by EUR 300–500 per tonne of aluminium before any abatement investment.

4. CONCLUSION AND OUTLOOK

Indonesia's electricity emission factor is spatially heterogeneous to a degree that national reporting conceals. Including industrial self-generation raises the factor by 38 % in Sulawesi, 40 % in Papua and 27 % in Maluku while leaving Java–Bali unchanged, and provincial factors span a 3.1-fold range. Under the CBAM definitive regime this heterogeneity is priced, varying the indirect liability on unwrought aluminium by EUR 324 per tonne between the cleanest and dirtiest zone.

The central finding concerns incentives rather than levels. Because the distribution is bimodal and the gap between its modes exceeds the scheduled mark-up, a country-level default makes verification unprofitable for producers in the five zones hosting the captive-coal fleet, while penalising the cleanest producers by up to EUR 165 per tonne. Combined with the exclusion of captive plants from the domestic trading scheme, the most carbon-intensive segment of Indonesia's export industry faces the weakest transparency incentive and the smallest relative cost.

Three research questions follow. How closely do capacity-based zonal factors track metered dispatch, and can the estimator be calibrated against officially published system factors? Does the inversion identified here also arise in other ASEAN member states with significant captive industrial power, which would make sub-national emission factors a regional rather than a national priority under APAEC 2026–2030? And at what spatial resolution, substation cluster or province, does an MRV-grade factor become both defensible to a CBAM verifier and administratively feasible for the national registry?

papers.abstract: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) entered its definitive regime on 1 January 2026, pricing the indirect emissions embedded in electricity used to produce imported aluminium, steel, cement and fertilisers. Exporters may either accept a country-level default value or verify an installation-specific actual value. This study shows that where national carbon intensity is spatially bimodal, that binary choice inverts the incentive it was designed to create. We compile a georeferenced inventory of 526 generating units (95.4 GW) and 933 transmission substations across Indonesia's eight interconnected systems, separate grid-connected from captive industrial self-generation using an auditable registry, and estimate zonal emission factors with Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation. Captive units hold 17.7 % of capacity but 27.6 % of generation-side CO2. Including them raises the Sulawesi emission factor by 38 %, Papua by 40 % and Maluku by 27 %, while leaving Java–Bali unchanged; provincial factors span a 3.1-fold range. At EUR 75.36/tCO2 the indirect charge on unwrought aluminium varies by EUR 324 per tonne between zones. Producers in five of eight zones, covering the entire nickel-processing captive belt, would pay more by verifying than by accepting the default.

The Balance Sheet Problem: Why Battery-Swapping Networks Migrate to Public Ownership

Qashtalani Haramaini

Monash University Indonesia · RACE for 2030 · [insert email]

IAEE Energy Specialization Code: 10.3 Transportation – Electric vehicles & systems

Summary of Research

Battery swapping is repeatedly proposed as the solution to the two problems that constrain electric vehicle adoption in emerging economies: the upfront cost of the battery, which represents 35–50 per cent of vehicle price, and the charging time that removes a vehicle from revenue service. Yet the record is sharply divided. Better Place failed in 2013 after roughly USD 850 million; Tesla demonstrated swapping the same year and abandoned it; Ample entered bankruptcy in December 2025 despite USD 270 million raised and partnerships with Shell, Mitsubishi and Stellantis. Over the same period Gogoro built a network serving 92 per cent of Taiwan’s electric two-wheelers, and NIO built more than 3,800 stations in China. The conventional explanations — technology readiness, standardisation, consumer acceptance — do not separate these outcomes cleanly, because several failed ventures had the technology, and several successful ones lacked a standard.

This paper argues that the dividing line is a question of energy economics rather than engineering, and that it concerns who holds the asset. A swap network must own an inventory of batteries larger than the vehicle fleet it serves. That inventory is a capital stock whose carrying cost scales with network size rather than with utilisation, which inverts the economics familiar from charging infrastructure. The paper tests, across national cases, which combinations of conditions allow that capital stock to be carried — and shows that in the largest cases the answer has been a public or quasi-public balance sheet. The question is significant because governments across MENA and Asia are currently committing sovereign and utility capital to charging, storage and hydrogen assets with the same structure, and are doing so without an evidence base on when that commitment is a necessary condition rather than a subsidy.

Methodology

The outcome of interest is configurational: a national swap network does not fail because one variable is too low, but because one required condition is absent while others are present. This rules out both meta-analysis, which requires comparable effect sizes that this literature does not contain, and regression designs, which assume additive and symmetric causation. The study therefore combines two methods.

(i) Fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) over 16–20 national cases, including historical failures (Israel, Denmark, United States) so that the design is not conditioned on survival. Eight conditions are calibrated from public statistics with pre-specified anchors: share of two- and three-wheelers in the fleet; commercial fleet share of target vehicles; presence of a binding pack interoperability mandate; supply-side concentration permitting a de facto standard; urban density; scarcity of home charging; legal and fiscal neutrality of battery–vehicle ownership decoupling; and availability of patient or public capital. fsQCA distinguishes necessary conditions from sufficient configurations and reports consistency and coverage, allowing equifinal paths to be identified rather than averaged away.

(ii) A common break-even model applied uniformly to every case, so that success is computed rather than inferred from corporate communication. Station-level break-even throughput is N* = (C·CRF + O + B·δ) / (p − c·e), where C is station capital cost, CRF the capital recovery factor, O annual operating cost, B the value of resident battery inventory, δ its degradation and financing rate, p the price per swap, c the electricity tariff and e energy per swap. The B·δ term is the structural difference between swapping and charging and is routinely omitted; its inclusion is what makes the ownership question tractable, and its sensitivity to the electricity tariff is what places the problem within energy economics.

Results and Findings

Preliminary coding of the evidence base yields three findings, reported here in advance of the full calibrated solution.

First, throughput separates the surviving networks from the struggling ones by vehicle segment, not by technology. Gogoro reports approximately 370,000 daily swaps across around 2,700 stations, or roughly 137 swaps per station per day. NIO completed over one million swaps during the seven-day May 2026 holiday across 3,851 stations — approximately 37 per station per day at a national peak-travel period, against an independent break-even estimate near 61. The two-wheeler network operates at roughly 3.7 times the per-station throughput of the four-wheeler network, and it is the two-wheeler network that has reached positive operating cash flow.

Second, the largest networks did not resolve the capital problem commercially; they relocated it. NIO has invested over CNY 20 billion in charging and swap infrastructure since 2018 and states that the swap business is not independently profitable. In August 2026 its swap assets began transferring to a state-owned enterprise, following an earlier asset-holding vehicle formed with a provincial energy group and a battery manufacturer. Gogoro reached its fifth consecutive quarter of positive operating cash flow in mid-2026 only after governance passed from founder to investor control and strategy shifted from expansion to cost containment. In both cases the network survived by changing whose balance sheet carried the battery inventory.

Third, the failures share a configuration, and it is not the inverse of the successes. Every consumer-facing, multi-manufacturer, passenger-car swap venture in a market with abundant home charging has failed, irrespective of capital raised or technical sophistication. Where a household can charge overnight at a domestic tariff, a swap priced near fast-charging rates offers no durable advantage. Conversely, where the vehicle is a production asset with monetised downtime, swapping wins even without an enforced standard. India illustrates the boundary precisely: swapping has been adopted across commercial two- and three-wheeler fleets, while none of the four largest consumer scooter manufacturers offers network-swappable batteries. Two named frictions persist there — the absence of a binding interoperability mandate despite policy drafting since 2022, and a tax asymmetry in which standalone batteries attract 18 per cent GST against 5 per cent for a complete vehicle, penalising every model that separates battery from vehicle.

Conclusions

The viability of battery swapping is determined by fleet utilisation and by who can carry the battery inventory, not by charging speed. Three conclusions follow for policy.

Battery swapping should be evaluated as an energy asset ownership question rather than a refuelling technology. The relevant appraisal variable is the carrying cost of resident inventory, which scales with network coverage and is therefore worsened, not improved, by coverage-driven deployment targets.

For emerging economies with motorcycle-dominant fleets, the binding constraint is usually enforced pack interoperability, not station count or purchase subsidy. Indonesia satisfies most conditions in the framework — motorcycle dominance, large ride-hail and delivery fleets, dense urban housing without domestic charging access, legal recognition of battery leasing, and a state utility able to hold assets — but lacks a binding standard. Units deployed before that mandate exists are built into incompatible networks that will require replacement, which is a fiscal argument for sequencing standardisation ahead of deployment.

For the MENA region the finding transfers unevenly, and the paper says so. Gulf passenger-vehicle markets satisfy few of the identified conditions, and the framework predicts that consumer swapping there would fail. Two applications remain strong: heavy-duty and mining fleets, where continuous utilisation restores the economics and where dedicated heavy-truck swap networks are already scaling in China; and the region’s substantial non-Gulf two- and three-wheeler economies, which share the structure of the Asian cases and are largely absent from the energy-economics literature. Most broadly, the ownership finding speaks directly to sovereign and utility investors currently deciding which long-payback energy assets they must hold themselves.

Bayesian models for spatial equity: separating latent demand from supply in EV charging infrastructure

Qashtalani Haramaini · PhD candidate · Monash University Indonesia · RACE for 2030 · Bayesian Analysis & Modelling Workshop 2026, PhD Poster Prize · Monash Caulfield, 18–19 November 2026

Demand that has never been built for is never observed. This study proposes a hierarchical framework that separates latent charging demand from the supply filter through which it is recorded — and propagates that uncertainty into the siting decision itself.

Poster utuh. Unduh versi PDF lewat tombol di atas untuk membacanya pada ukuran penuh.

Argumen dalam satu baris

Yang tercatatYang dimodelkanYang dipulihkanYang diputuskan
Sesi y — cacahan yang under-detected. Hanya permintaan yang bertemu charger menjadi data. Capture a × demand d, dipisahkan oleh kovariat sisi pasokan yang hanya menggerakkan a. Posterior untuk setiap wilayah — permintaan laten dengan ketidakpastian yang jujur, paling lebar di tempat rekaman paling tipis. P(permintaan tak terpenuhi > τ) — situs diperingkat menurut peluang pembangunan layak.

1. Pengamatan bersyarat pada pasokan

Infrastruktur pengisian ditempatkan di tempat utilisasi sudah tinggi, sehingga bukti yang dipakai perencana adalah sampel yang diseleksi oleh keputusan yang hendak diinformasikannya. Hasilnya memperkuat diri sendiri: kapasitas mengalir ke daerah yang sudah punya, permintaan laten di tempat lain tetap tak terlihat karena tidak pernah menjadi sesi, dan keadilan lalu dinilai di atas rekaman yang sama — yang membuat permintaan tampak jauh lebih terkonsentrasi daripada sebenarnya.

2. Mengapa masalah ini Bayesian, bukan sekadar difit

  • Kelangkaan tidak punya jawaban maximum-likelihood. Sebagian besar unit mencatat nol sesi karena memang nol charger; laju tingkat-wilayah tak terdefinisi atau sangat tidak stabil. Prior hierarkis meminjam kekuatan dari tetangga alih-alih membuang unitnya.
  • Struktur spasial adalah parameter, bukan gangguan. Reparameterisasi BYM2 memisahkan heterogenitas terstruktur dari tak terstruktur di bawah parameter pencampur ρ yang dapat ditafsirkan.
  • Keputusan butuh probabilitas, bukan estimasi titik. Komite penempatan seharusnya menanyakan P(permintaan tak terpenuhi > ambang kelayakan), yang dikembalikan posterior secara langsung.
  • Indeks ketimpangan adalah fungsional non-linear. Gini dan Lorenz atas laju terestimasi tidak punya galat baku analitik yang bersih; draw posterior meneruskan ketidakpastian menembusnya secara tepat.

3. Model: permintaan dan capture, diestimasi bersama

Struktur imperfect-detection (N-mixture) kanonik: sesi teramati yi adalah permintaan penduduk laten di yang ditipiskan oleh probabilitas capture ai ∈ (0,1), ditambah aliran koridor ci untuk lalu lintas lintas-wilayah.

  • Observasi — yi ~ NegBin(μi, φ), μi = di · ai + ci; ci hanya bukan-nol di wilayah berkoridor tol.
  • Permintaan laten — log di = β₀ + xiᵀβ + ui + vi (armada EV terdaftar, instalasi pengisian rumah, populasi & kepadatan aktivitas, pembangkitan perjalanan, pendapatan, campuran POI).
  • Saringan capture — logit ai = γ₀ + ziᵀγ: hanya sisi pasokan — jarak ke gardu tegangan menengah dengan kapasitas cadangan, ketersediaan lahan, waktu tempuh penduduk ke charger terdekat, topologi jaringan, bukan preferensi pengemudi.
  • Prior spasial BYM2 — u + v = τ−½(√ρ · u* + √(1−ρ) · v*), u* ~ ICAR(W), v* ~ N(0,1); prior PC pada τ dan φ; ρ ~ Beta(½, ½).

4. Masalah identifikasi, dinyatakan terus terang

Tidak ada dalam data yang membedakan permintaan rendah, terlayani baik dari permintaan tinggi, nyaris tak terlayani: keduanya menghasilkan sedikit sesi. Memisahkan d dari a menuntut argumen, bukan data lebih banyak. Argumennya adalah exclusion restriction: headroom jaringan dan ketersediaan lahan menentukan di mana charger secara fisik dapat dibangun; keduanya tidak membawa informasi tentang apakah pengemudi di wilayah itu ingin mengisi. Keduanya menggerakkan a, bukan d. Asumsi inilah mata rantai terlemah dan diperlakukan sebagai demikian: analisis sensitivitas prior atas γ, kalibrasi berbasis simulasi pada data sintetik dengan d diketahui, dan uji pemalsuan pada wilayah yang pasokannya meluas karena alasan tak berkaitan dengan permintaan.

5. Latar dan data — Jawa Barat

Jawa Barat: 27 kota dan kabupaten, ±50 juta penduduk, front paling aktif dari roll-out pengisian publik Indonesia. Rekaman Maret 2026 terurai menjadi 14 wilayah layanan operator (41,1 juta penduduk, 633 unit charger); analisis dilakukan pada tingkat wilayah layanan, dengan disagregasi lebih halus pada grid 1 km sebagai tahap berikutnya.

6. Indeks keadilan yang mempertahankan ketidakpastiannya

Dua ketidakadilan harus dipisahkan: ketimpangan akses (pasokan terkonsentrasi di sedikit wilayah) dan ketimpangan permintaan tak terpenuhi (kebutuhan tertinggal tanpa layanan). Hanya yang kedua menunjukkan di mana intervensi mengubah kesejahteraan. Keduanya lazim dilaporkan sebagai satu angka Gini; karena kuantitas yang mendasarinya diestimasi, indeksnya adalah distribusi posterior dan lebarnya adalah selisih antara pembelaan yang dapat dipertahankan dan hiasan belaka.

7. Kesimpulan: apa yang dibeli perlakuan Bayesian

Temuan. Dipasang pada rekaman Maret 2026 — 101.020 sesi, 633 unit charger, 14 wilayah layanan, 41,1 juta penduduk — model mengembalikan permintaan laten agregat 229.000 kejadian melawan 101.020 yang tercatat (selisih ×2,3). Capture permintaan penduduk membentang 0,15–0,72 antar-wilayah (agregat 0,42 setelah dikurangi ±4.800 sesi aliran koridor); rasio celah berkisar 0,7×–6,6×. Sesi teramati terdistribusi lebih timpang (G = 0,41) daripada permintaan terestimasi (G = 0,33). Permintaan tak terpenuhi setelah penyesuaian kapasitas ≈2.260 kejadian/hari.

Susunan spasial. Ketiga indeks Gini terurut jelas: penyediaan charger paling timpang (G = 0,19 — catatan poster), sesi teramati paling terkonsentrasi (G = 0,41). Konsentrasi dalam rekaman karena itu dihasilkan oleh capture, bukan oleh tempat orang tinggal — koridor tol terlayani berlebih sementara wilayah pedalaman berpenduduk padat kurang terlayani.

Metodologis. Model gabungan permintaan–capture dengan struktur spasial BYM2 mengubah rekaman operator yang under-detected menjadi estimasi permintaan penduduk yang rekaman itu sendiri tidak bisa menunjukkannya — dengan indeks ketimpangan yang membawa selang kredibel.

Praktis. Memeringkat wilayah kandidat atas sesi mentah hanya mereproduksi peta pasokan yang sudah ada; memeringkatnya atas P(permintaan tak terpenuhi > τ) tidak. Kedua urutan berbeda secara material: Indramayu naik dari dasar tabel sesi ke peringkat 6 dan menjadi wilayah yang layak diselidiki meski hanya mencatat 1.508 sesi — dekat Purwakarta dan Cirebon yang sibuk dalam rekaman tetapi jatuh ke separuh bawah begitu capture diperhitungkan.

Rekomendasi

  1. Tempatkan atas permintaan tak terpenuhi, bukan atas sesi. Memeringkat wilayah kandidat atas P(permintaan tak terpenuhi > τ) menaikkan Indramayu dari dasar ke peringkat 6 dan menjadikannya layak diselidiki hanya atas 1.508 sesi tercatat.

One Model, Two Cities: The Objective Function as an Unaccountable Planning Decision in Algorithmic EV Charging Deployment

Qashtalani Haramaini — Monash University Indonesia (RACE for 2030 Program) / PT PLN (Persero) UID Jawa Barat, Indonesia — qashtalani.haramaini@monash.edu (corresponding and presenting author) · Alyas Widita — Monash University Indonesia — alyas.widita@monash.edu · Liz Taylor — Monash University, Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture (MADA), Australia — liz.taylor@monash.edu

CUPUM 2027 — Future Cities in the Era of AI · Book chapter (full manuscript draft)

Abstract

Public electric-vehicle (EV) charging in Indonesia is allocated not by a planning authority but by a siting model inside the vertically integrated state utility. This chapter treats that model as an object of planning inquiry. Using a random forest fitted to 101,020 charging sessions at 330 public sites and a Bayesian exposure model of 3,687 registered EV owners in West Java, we build a reproducible siting pipeline on a 5 km grid and then run it under two objective functions: a commercial lens that maximises predicted energy yield and an equity lens that weights unserved owners, distance to existing chargers and regency income. The same evidence and the same 50-site budget produce two different provinces. The commercial portfolio concentrates in 9 regencies, places 20 per cent of sites in low-income regencies and reaches 577 currently unserved owners; the equity portfolio spreads over 14 regencies, places 54 per cent of sites in low-income regencies and reaches 723 owners, at a cost of 42 per cent of model-predicted energy. Only 21 sites appear in both. A continuous sweep of the equity weight shows the trade-off is smooth and monotonic: a political choice rendered as a parameter. We argue that where no planning authority allocates infrastructure, the objective function is land-use policy, and propose a minimum accountability standard: publish the objective and its weights, publish at least one counterfactual portfolio, name who each objective excludes, and version the model. Disclosure of the objective function is the functional substitute for a planning process.

Keywords: electric vehicle charging; algorithmic accountability; spatial justice; planning support systems; Global South; Indonesia

1. Introduction

Cities are increasingly planned by systems that were never designed as planning instruments. A recommender for where to place a bus stop, a scoring model for which streets receive lighting, a demand forecast that decides which neighbourhood receives the next substation: each encodes a judgement about who deserves what, and each is usually written by engineers, calibrated to data, and never subjected to the procedures that a zoning decision or a transport plan would face. The computational urban planning literature has long argued that planning support systems (PSS) should make such judgements visible and contestable (Geertman and Stillwell, 2020; Pettit et al., 2018). This chapter examines a case in which the PSS has quietly replaced the planning process altogether.

Public EV charging in Indonesia is that case. Presidential Regulation 55/2019 launched the national battery-EV programme and assigned the roll-out of public charging stations (SPKLU) to the state electricity company, PT PLN (Persero). PLN is vertically integrated: it operates the distribution network, sells the electricity, and owns or anchors most public chargers through a partnership scheme. In West Java, Indonesia's most populous province with 49.9 million residents, there is no provincial or municipal instrument that allocates charging capacity across its 27 cities and regencies. Where a charger is built is decided inside the utility, using an internal multi-criteria siting model that ranks candidate locations on predicted demand, points of interest, population and distance to existing stations. No public hearing, no zoning review and no appeal mechanism governs that ranking.

The consequence is that the objective function inside the siting model has become a land-use policy. Its weights decide whether the next tranche of public capital densifies the Jakarta commuter belt or reaches the southern regencies; whether it follows toll corridors or follows households. In Sovacool and Dworkin's (2015) vocabulary, this is a distributive outcome produced by a procedural choice, except that the procedure is four numbers in a configuration file and the choice was never disclosed.

This chapter makes that choice visible. It has three aims. First, it documents a computational siting pipeline that is in operational use in a Global South megaregion, built on operator data that urban researchers rarely obtain: session-level charging transactions, the transformer asset register, and a geocoded register of households that applied for the home-charging tariff. Second, it demonstrates counterfactual portfolio analysis as a technique for making objective functions legible: the same model, the same budget, run under a commercial and an equity objective, with the difference between the two portfolios mapped and quantified. Third, it argues for a minimum accountability standard for algorithmic infrastructure siting, and shows what that standard would have revealed here. The empirical work is fully reproducible from a public repository; every figure below is recomputed from the raw data.

The chapter responds directly to CUPUM 2027's call for work that pairs technical rigour with critical reflection, and to its interest in spatial justice and computational urbanism beyond the usual Northern circuits. The Indonesian structure, one organisation holding both the grid and the chargers, is not an exotic exception. It is the structure of most state utilities in Asia, Africa and Latin America, and it is where the next several hundred thousand public chargers will be sited by models nobody outside the utility can see.

2. Background: siting models as planning instruments

2.1 From optimisation to allocation

The academic literature on charging-station siting is large and overwhelmingly framed as optimisation. Flow-refuelling and set-covering formulations locate stations to intercept traffic or minimise access distance (Kuby and Lim, 2005); GIS multi-criteria overlays rank candidate parcels on weighted layers (Malczewski, 2006; Csiszár et al., 2019); machine-learning models predict utilisation from land use and demographics (Pagany et al., 2019). Pagany et al.'s review of 133 localisation studies finds that almost all take the objective as given and treat the weights as an analyst's choice. That is a reasonable stance in a paper. It is not a reasonable stance in a utility that will build what the model recommends.

A separate literature documents that public charger access is unequally distributed. In California, block groups with below-median income and Black or Hispanic majorities are significantly less likely to contain any public charger (Hsu and Fingerman, 2021); nationally in the United States, the gap persists after controlling for vehicle ownership (Lou et al., 2024); across Europe, access clusters with commercial land use and motorway corridors (Falchetta and Noussan, 2021; Carlton and Sultana, 2022). Roy and Law (2022) use machine learning to show that placement in the United States is predicted by affluence even after accounting for demand. These studies treat the allocation mechanism as a market outcome. In a state-utility setting the mechanism is a model, and the model can be opened.

2.2 Planning support systems and the problem of the black box

The PSS tradition has always been concerned with the legibility of models to planners and publics. Geertman and Stillwell (2020) trace three decades of effort to close the gap between what models can compute and what planning processes can absorb; Pettit et al. (2018) show that scenario-based PSS can be adopted when they make alternative futures comparable rather than prescribing one. Batty (2013) frames the underlying epistemology: a model is a hypothesis about the city, and its value lies in the comparison of hypotheses, not in a single output. The counterfactual method in this chapter is an application of that principle to an operational model.

The algorithmic-accountability literature adds the governance layer. Kroll et al. (2017) argue that accountability for automated decisions requires more than transparency of code; it requires procedures that let affected parties contest outcomes. Ananny and Crawford (2018) caution that 'seeing inside' a system does not by itself produce accountability. Yeung (2018) distinguishes algorithmic regulation that steers behaviour from regulation of algorithms that constrains the steering. Diakopoulos (2016) proposes concrete disclosure elements for public-sector algorithms. What none of these authors addresses is the case where the algorithm is not making a decision within a policy but is the policy, because no other allocation instrument exists. That is the gap this chapter addresses.

2.3 The Indonesian setting

Indonesia's EV programme is young and fast. Battery-EV sales roughly doubled in 2025 to about 107,000 units, and the PLN public-charging network grew 44 per cent in a year to 4,655 units at 3,007 locations (IEA, 2025). EV penetration remains below one per cent of the vehicle stock, so charging is being built ahead of demand: the regime in which the siting objective matters most, because there is no observed usage to discipline it. PLN's dominance means that the model documented here is not one operator's tool among many; it is, for most of the province, the allocation mechanism.

3. Case, data and the deployed model

3.1 Data

Three datasets were assembled from PLN UID Jawa Barat, the distribution unit for West Java, and one from public sources (Table 1). The charging log contains every session at PLN's public chargers in March 2026: 101,020 transactions at 636 charging units across 348 registered sites, of which 330 have valid coordinates, totalling 2.26 GWh. The EV customer register lists 3,687 geocoded households that applied for the home-charging tariff between November 2025 and June 2026; because these households were registered by vehicle ownership rather than by proximity to a public charger, the register is an exposure proxy for latent demand that is independent of where chargers were built. The transformer register provides 53,797 distribution-transformer records with location, rated capacity and loading, of which 41,129 pass plausibility checks; it is used here for a feasibility screen (headroom at the 80 per cent planning limit) and as a density covariate. City and regency population, Human Development Index and income tier come from Statistics Indonesia (BPS) and the provincial Klassen typology.

3.2 The deployed siting tool

The operational tool, built in ArcGIS for the 2026 Esri Indonesia Fellowship, works in three stages. A random forest trained on the transaction log predicts station-level energy sales for candidate locations, with SHAP attribution (Lundberg and Lee, 2017) used to identify the dominant predictors. Predicted demand is then composited with point-of-interest density, population and distance to the nearest existing station through a weighted overlay (weights 0.35, 0.30, 0.25 and 0.20 respectively) on a 2 km hexagonal grid, producing a suitability index over 490 candidate cells. Served area is defined by a 10-minute network drive-time isochrone rather than a Euclidean buffer. The tool's headline output is a ranked build order of 244 locations projected to sell 12.6 GWh a year; in that projection the ten highest-ranked locations carry 46.4 per cent of projected energy and the top fifty carry 92.7 per cent. The weights were set by the analyst. They were reviewed by nobody outside the project.

3.3 A reproducible counterfactual pipeline

To make the objective function contestable, the chapter rebuilds the pipeline in open code on a coarser 0.045° (≈5 km) grid of 1,295 cells, so that every result can be recomputed from the raw data without the proprietary POI layer. The rebuild preserves the logic of the deployed tool while replacing its unpublishable inputs. Its components are as follows.

Observed-data predictor. A random forest (Breiman, 2001) is fitted on the 174 cells that contain at least one charger, with log energy sold in March 2026 as the target and six covariates available for every cell in the province: installed transformer capacity (kVA), transformer count, growth-corrected headroom, latitude, longitude and distance to the nearest existing charger. This is deliberately the model a utility would build from what it already holds: transactions, the grid and geography. Out-of-bag R² is 0.18; the predictor is weak in absolute terms, which is itself informative, and it is used only to rank.

Yield calibration. For the 132 cells that have registered EV owners but no charger (908 owners), an expected monthly energy is also computed as owners multiplied by a regency-specific yield intensity, the observed energy per registered owner in served cells of the same regency, bounded to between one quarter and four times the provincial mean of 812 kWh per owner. This gives a second, register-based yield estimate that does not depend on the random forest.

Feasibility. A cell is eligible only if aggregate transformer headroom at the 80 per cent limit, corrected for load growth to March 2026, is at least 240 kVA, sufficient for one four-charger 60 kW site; 21 of the 132 candidate cells fail this screen.

Two objective functions. The commercial lens ranks eligible cells by the observed-data predictor's expected energy, standardised as a z-score of log predicted kWh. The equity lens is a weighted sum of three standardised terms: log registered owners in the cell (weight 0.4), distance to the nearest existing charger (0.3) and a regency need score set to 1 for low-income, 0.5 for medium-income and 0 for high-income regencies under the provincial Klassen typology (0.3). A blended score with equity weight λ ∈ [0, 1] interpolates between them; λ = 0 is purely commercial and λ = 1 purely equity-oriented. Under each λ the 50 highest-scoring eligible cells are selected.

Outcome metrics. For each portfolio the chapter reports: unserved registered owners newly reached; model-predicted energy; regencies covered; share of sites in low-income regencies; sites in cells with below-median registered demand (a proxy for stranded capital); provincial coverage, defined as the share of registered owners living in a cell with a charger; and the between-regency Gini of coverage, following the Lorenz-curve tradition in transport equity (Delbosc and Currie, 2011). Regency assignment for cells uses a nine-nearest-neighbour vote over labelled EV customer and site points.

4. Results

4.1 The geography of demand and supply

Figure 1. Registered EV owners per 5 km cell (blue, log scale) and public charging sites sized by March 2026 energy sales (orange). Owners cluster in the Jakarta commuter belt (Depok, Bogor, Bekasi) and Greater Bandung; a secondary corridor runs east along the toll road to Cirebon.

Figure 1 sets the stage. Registered EV owners are concentrated in two metropolitan cores and one corridor; public chargers follow the same pattern but with a long tail of low-yield sites at PLN offices across the province. Of 3,687 registered owners, 75 per cent already live in a cell with at least one charger, but the between-regency coverage Gini is 0.24: coverage is near-complete in Bekasi and Depok and fragmentary in the southern regencies.

4.2 Yield is concentrated, and concentration is where the commercial objective lives

Figure 2. (a) Cumulative share of March 2026 energy across 330 sites ranked by yield. (b) Mean energy per site by host-location type; n is the number of sites of that type.

Figure 2(a) shows why the objective function matters. Across the 330 existing sites, the ten busiest sold 27.6 per cent of all energy, the busiest fifty sold 73.9 per cent and the busiest hundred 91.9 per cent; the site-level Gini of energy is 0.77. Figure 2(b) shows the mechanism: toll-road rest areas average 18.7 MWh a month per site, dealer showrooms 17.3 MWh, while the 132 PLN office sites, 40 per cent of the network, average 5.3 MWh and hotels 1.4 MWh. Any model trained on this record learns that yield lives on the motorway and in the showroom. A commercial objective will send capital there, and it will be right, in its own terms, to do so.

4.3 Two objectives, two provinces

Figure 3. Fifty new sites selected from the same 111 eligible cells under (a) the commercial objective and (b) the equity objective. Grey dots are existing sites; pink shading marks low-income regencies. Only 21 cells appear in both portfolios.

Figure 3 and Table 2 are the core of the chapter. Given the same eligible cells and the same budget of 50 sites, the commercial objective selects a portfolio that hugs the existing network: 18 sites in Bogor, 13 in Bekasi, none in Bandung, Sukabumi, Garut or Tasikmalaya. It reaches 577 of the 908 unserved registered owners, spreads over 9 regencies, places 10 sites in low-income regencies, and puts 18 of its 50 sites in cells with below-median registered demand, because the observed-data predictor rewards grid density and proximity to the metropolitan core regardless of who lives there. The equity objective selects a portfolio that reaches 723 owners, 25 per cent more, over 14 regencies with 27 sites in low-income regencies, including 7 in Sukabumi and 4 in Bandung, and lowers the between-regency coverage Gini from 0.24 today to 0.14, against 0.18 under the commercial objective. Its cost, in the model's own currency, is 42 per cent less predicted energy.
