Two features of Table 2 deserve emphasis. First, neither portfolio is wrong. The commercial portfolio is a defensible optimisation of the utility's revenue; the equity portfolio is a defensible optimisation of the province's access. Both are produced from identical evidence by an identical machine. Second, the two portfolios disagree about most of the map: only 21 of 50 cells are common to both. A regency such as Sukabumi, with 3.2 million residents and a low-income classification, receives 7 sites under one objective and none under the other. That is not a technical detail. It is a decision about whether one of the largest regencies in Java is part of the electric-mobility transition in the next investment cycle.

4.4 A political choice rendered as a parameter

Figure 4. Sweeping the equity weight λ from 0 (commercial) to 1 (equity): (a) model-predicted energy of the 50-site portfolio; (b) share of sites in low-income regencies; (c) between-regency coverage Gini, with today's value as the dashed line.

Figure 4 sweeps λ in steps of 0.1. The trade-off is smooth. Predicted energy falls slowly until λ ≈ 0.6 and then steeply; the share of sites in low-income regencies rises from 20 to 54 per cent; the coverage Gini falls in two steps, at λ ≈ 0.5 and λ ≈ 1. There is no natural breakpoint, no value of λ that the data select. Every point on the curve is a different province, and the choice among them is exactly the kind of choice that planning processes exist to make: how much revenue the utility should forgo to reach households in Sukabumi and Garut. In the deployed tool that choice is made by whoever last edited the weight table. The chapter's claim is not that the current weights are wrong. It is that they are a policy, and that policies are supposed to be visible.

5. Discussion

5.1 What the counterfactual reveals that the model does not

A siting model reports a ranking. A ranking hides its own alternatives. Running the same model under a second objective and mapping the difference is a cheap operation, a few lines of code against a pipeline that already exists, and it converts an opaque recommendation into a legible trade-off. In this case it reveals that the commercial objective would not place a single site in four regencies with a combined population of 14 million; that the equity objective would reach a quarter more currently unserved owners; and that the price of doing so is 42 per cent of predicted energy from 50 sites, or roughly 89 MWh a month, on a network that sells 2,260 MWh a month today. That is a number a provincial government could argue about. It is not a number the current process produces.

5.2 A minimum accountability standard for algorithmic infrastructure siting

The findings translate into four requirements that a public utility, or the regulator that licenses it, could adopt without changing who owns the chargers. First, publish the objective function and its weights, in the same way that EU system operators must now publish the criteria behind hosting-capacity maps. Second, publish at least one counterfactual portfolio under an alternative objective, so that the distributive content of the chosen objective is visible rather than implicit. Third, name the population that each objective excludes: the regencies that receive no site, the owners who remain unserved, the income tiers that lose share. Fourth, version the model and its weights, so that a ranking that misdirected public capital can be traced to the configuration that produced it and corrected rather than trusted. These requirements echo Diakopoulos's (2016) disclosure elements and Kroll et al.'s (2017) insistence on contestability, but they are specific to the situation in which the algorithm is the allocation instrument. They are also cheap: everything in this chapter was produced from data the utility already holds.

5.3 Publication as the substitute for a planning process

Where a planning authority exists, a siting model is an input to it and the authority can be lobbied. Where none exists, the model is the authority. Kitchin (2014) warns that data-driven urbanism tends to present political choices as technical ones; Shelton et al. (2015) show that the actually existing smart city is assembled from precisely such unexamined defaults. The Indonesian charging roll-out is an unusually pure instance, because the organisation running the model also owns the grid, the chargers and the customer data, and because the model is running ahead of any observed demand that could discipline it. In that structure, disclosure of the objective function is not a transparency nicety. It is the functional substitute for a planning process: the only point at which a province, a regency or a civil-society group could see what the utility is optimising for and ask it to optimise for something else.

5.4 Limitations

The counterfactual is built on a 5 km grid and an open-data rebuild of the deployed tool; the operational model uses a 2 km hexagon grid and a proprietary POI layer that cannot be published, so the portfolios shown are illustrative of the deployed tool's logic rather than reproductions of its output. The observed-data predictor is weak (out-of-bag R² of 0.18), which is a finding about the predictability of yield from grid and geography alone, but it means the commercial ranking carries substantial noise. Registered home-charging customers under-represent households without off-street parking, who may depend most on public chargers; the equity lens therefore understates need in dense urban kampung. The equity objective is one of many that could be written, and the chapter does not claim it is the right one; its role is to show that any second objective exposes the first. Finally, the 50-site budget is a device; the deployed tool ranks 244 sites, and the shape of the trade-off at that scale is a matter for the full study.

6. Conclusion

In West Java the question of who gets public EV charging has moved from the planning office, where it never was, to the objective function of a siting model inside the state utility. This chapter has shown that the model, run under two defensible objectives on identical evidence, produces two different provinces: one that densifies the Jakarta commuter belt and one that reaches the southern regencies, differing in 29 of 50 sites, in whether Sukabumi and Bandung receive any site at all, and in 42 per cent of predicted energy. The difference is a parameter. It should be a policy. Publishing the objective function, the counterfactual it suppresses and the population it excludes is the least a utility can do when its model has become the only planning instrument a province has, and it is also, on this evidence, enough to turn a black box into an argument that can be had in public.

papers.abstract: Public electric-vehicle (EV) charging in Indonesia is allocated not by a planning authority but by a siting model inside the vertically integrated state utility. This chapter treats that model as an object of planning inquiry. Using a random forest fitted to 101,020 charging sessions at 330 public sites and a Bayesian exposure model of 3,687 registered EV owners in West Java, we build a reproducible siting pipeline on a 5 km grid and then run it under two objective functions: a commercial lens that maximises predicted energy yield and an equity lens that weights unserved owners, distance to existing chargers and regency income. The same evidence and the same 50-site budget produce two different provinces. The commercial portfolio concentrates in 9 regencies, places 20 per cent of sites in low-income regencies and reaches 577 currently unserved owners; the equity portfolio spreads over 14 regencies, places 54 per cent of sites in low-income regencies and reaches 723 owners, at a cost of 42 per cent of model-predicted energy. Only 21 sites appear in both. A continuous sweep of the equity weight shows the trade-off is smooth and monotonic: a political choice rendered as a parameter. We argue that where no planning authority allocates infrastructure, the objective function is land-use policy, and propose a minimum accountability standard: publish the objective and its weights, publish at least one counterfactual portfolio, name who each objective excludes, and version the model. Disclosure of the objective function is the functional substitute for a planning process.

papers.html:
Training on the Past: Feedback Loops, Latent Demand and the Politics of Sparse Data in Charging Networks

Qashtalani Haramaini — Monash University Indonesia (RACE for 2030 Program) / PT PLN (Persero) UID Jawa Barat, Indonesia — qashtalani.haramaini@monash.edu (corresponding and presenting author) · Alyas Widita — Monash University Indonesia — alyas.widita@monash.edu · Liz Taylor — Monash University, Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture (MADA), Australia — liz.taylor@monash.edu

CUPUM 2027 — Future Cities in the Era of AI · Book chapter (full manuscript draft)

Abstract

In a network built ahead of demand, the transaction record a siting model learns from is not a sample of demand but a record of previous allocation decisions. This chapter shows, with operator data from West Java, Indonesia, that the conventional data-driven siting pipeline contains a feedback loop with distributive consequences. Observed transactions exist in only 174 of 1295 five-kilometre cells; 132 cells hold 908 registered EV owners and no charger. We compare two models on the same territory: a random forest fitted to observed transactions using grid and geographic covariates, and a Gamma–Poisson hierarchical model of latent demand that partially pools an exposure signal independent of charger placement, 3,687 households registered for the home-charging tariff. The models agree only weakly on where to build next (Spearman ρ = 0.30; 26 of the top 50 cells in common), and posterior uncertainty is widest exactly where no infrastructure and no observation exist. A deployment simulation shows why the difference compounds: demand from unserved cells is credited to the nearest served site, and a model retrained on that record keeps recommending densification. After ten rounds the observed-data rule leaves 19 per cent of latent demand in low-income regencies unserved against 7 per cent for the latent-demand rule. Sparsity is an artefact of an earlier distributive choice; treating missing data as missing demand launders that choice into a forecast. The chapter proposes an inferential design that separates exposure from observation and reports uncertainty as a first-class output of any planning support system.

Keywords: latent demand; Bayesian hierarchical modelling; feedback loops; data sparsity; algorithmic fairness; electric vehicle charging

1. Introduction

Every machine-learning model of urban demand is a model of the past. Charging-station siting models are trained on transaction logs, utilisation records and mobile-app check-ins; they learn where charging happens and recommend more of it. In a mature network, where nearly every plausible location has been tried, this is a reasonable procedure: the record approximates the demand surface. In a young network, built ahead of demand in a country where EVs are still below one per cent of the vehicle stock, the record is something else. It is the set of places where the utility chose to build, and nothing more. Places never served produce no transactions, and a model cannot learn that they should have been served from data that does not contain them.

This chapter argues that the standard data-driven siting pipeline therefore contains a feedback loop, structurally identical to the one Ensign et al. (2018) proved for predictive policing. There, police are dispatched to neighbourhoods where crime was previously discovered, discover more crime there because they are present, and the model that allocates them learns from the discoveries. Here, chargers are built where charging was previously observed, drivers from unserved neighbourhoods travel to those chargers, the sessions are logged at the served location, and the model that allocates the next tranche learns that demand lives where the chargers already are. Performative prediction (Perdomo et al., 2020) gives the general form: a model whose outputs change the distribution it will next be trained on. The novelty of this chapter is to demonstrate the loop with operator data, to quantify what it does to a real siting recommendation, and to show that a different inferential design can break it.

The setting is West Java, Indonesia's most populous province, where the state utility PLN operates both the distribution grid and most public chargers. Three datasets held by one organisation make the analysis possible: the complete charging log for March 2026, 101,020 sessions at 330 geocoded sites; the distribution transformer register, 53,797 records; and, crucially, a register of 3,687 households that applied for PLN's home-charging tariff, geocoded at the service point. The third dataset is the key. Households applied because they bought an EV, not because a public charger was nearby; the register is therefore an exposure proxy for latent demand that is statistically independent of the deployment decisions the transaction log reflects. Few utilities hold such a proxy and fewer researchers have seen one; it allows the feedback loop to be measured rather than merely asserted.

The chapter proceeds as follows. Section 2 positions the argument between the siting literature, which treats sparsity as a data-availability problem, and the algorithmic-fairness literature, which treats it as a source of bias. Section 3 describes the two models: an observed-data random forest and a Gamma–Poisson hierarchical latent-demand model with partial pooling across regencies. Section 4 reports how far they disagree, where the posterior is uncertain, and what happens when each is used to drive deployment over ten rounds. Section 5 draws the implications for planning support systems in data-sparse cities.

2. Background

2.1 Sparsity as a data problem

The siting literature is aware that observed usage is scarce in emerging markets. Pagany et al.'s (2019) review of localisation methods notes that most demand-based approaches rely on traffic counts, parking data or existing usage that are unavailable outside a handful of rich cities, and recommends proxies such as land use and points of interest. Csiszár et al. (2019) build a land-use-based method precisely for cities without usage data. The dominant framing is that sparsity limits what can be estimated, and that better proxies or more data will close the gap. Missing data are treated, in Rubin's (1976) terms, as missing at random: uninformative about the quantity being estimated once covariates are accounted for.

2.2 Sparsity as bias

The algorithmic-fairness literature reads the same situation differently. When the mechanism that generates observations depends on the outcome of earlier predictions, missingness is informative and the resulting estimates are biased in a direction that reinforces the earlier decision. Ensign et al. (2018) formalise this with an urn model and show that even a small initial disparity in discovery rates is amplified without limit. Perdomo et al. (2020) generalise to any predictor that influences its own future training distribution. Barocas et al. (2023) catalogue the selection mechanisms that produce such loops in lending, hiring and public services; Eubanks (2018) documents their human consequences in welfare administration. Applications to urban infrastructure are rare, and none to charging. Yet charging is close to the ideal case: allocation is made by a single actor, the outcome of allocation (sessions) is the training target of the next allocation, and users are mobile, so unserved demand is not lost but displaced onto served locations.

2.3 Exposure, observation and partial pooling

Statistical epidemiology solved a closely related problem decades ago. Disease counts in small areas are sparse and noisy; the raw rate in a district with three cases is uninformative. Clayton and Kaldor (1987) introduced empirical-Bayes smoothing of area rates towards a regional mean, and Besag, York and Mollié (1991) the spatial random-effects formulation that underlies modern disease mapping. The essential move is to separate exposure (population at risk) from observation (cases), and to let areas borrow strength from their neighbours in proportion to how little they have observed (Efron and Morris, 1975; Gelman and Hill, 2007). This chapter applies the same logic to charging demand, with registered EV owners as cases and electrified premises, proxied by transformer count, as exposure. The result is a model whose uncertainty is largest where it has seen least, which is the property a siting model in a sparse network most needs and most often lacks.

3. Data and models

3.1 The grid and the pattern of observation

All data were aggregated to a 0.045° (≈5 km) grid over West Java. Of 1,295 cells that contain at least one distribution transformer, 238 contain registered EV owners and 174 contain a public charger. The overlap is partial: 132 cells hold 908 registered owners, a quarter of the provincial total, and no charger. Classified by median demand and median network headroom, the high-demand/high-headroom quadrant holds 84.2 per cent of owners and 70.3 per cent of chargers; the roll-out is broadly rational. The high-demand/low-headroom quadrant holds 11.6 per cent of owners but 5.6 per cent of chargers, and 20 of its cells, with 230 owners, have no charger at all (Table 1). These are the cells a transaction-trained model has never seen.

3.2 Model A: the observed-data predictor

Model A is the model a utility builds from what it already holds. A random forest (Breiman, 2001; 500 trees, minimum leaf size 3) is fitted on the 174 served cells with log energy sold in March 2026 as the target and six covariates available everywhere: installed transformer capacity, transformer count, growth-corrected headroom, latitude, longitude and distance to the nearest charger. The EV customer register is deliberately excluded, because the purpose is to represent the conventional pipeline that does not have it. Out-of-bag R² is 0.18. The most important covariates are installed capacity (0.26), headroom (0.23) and the two coordinates (0.40 combined): the model has learned that yield is a function of grid density and of where in the province one is. That is an accurate description of the March 2026 record. It is also a description of the geography of previous investment.

3.3 Model B: latent demand with partial pooling

Model B separates exposure from observation. Let n_i be registered EV owners in cell i and E_i the number of distribution transformers, a proxy for electrified premises. We assume n_i ~ Poisson(θ_i E_i), where θ_i is the latent adoption rate per transformer, and θ_i ~ Gamma(α_r, β_r) with hyperparameters specific to regency r. The Gamma prior is conjugate, so the posterior is θ_i | n_i ~ Gamma(α_r + n_i, β_r + E_i), with posterior mean (α_r + n_i)/(β_r + E_i) and closed-form quantiles. Regency hyperparameters are set by the method of moments on the observed cell rates within each regency, shrunk towards the provincial moments with weight k/(k + 10) where k is the number of cells in the regency (Clayton and Kaldor, 1987). Latent demand in cell i is θ_i E_i; its 90 per cent posterior interval is reported as a relative width, (q95 − q05)/mean, so that cells with different exposure are comparable. Three properties matter. First, a cell with owners but no charger has a well-defined posterior, because the model never used chargers. Second, a cell with no owners does not receive a point estimate of zero; it receives the regency prior, with an interval that reflects how little was observed. Third, regencies with few cells borrow strength from the province rather than from their own noise.

3.4 Comparison and simulation

The two models are compared on the 132 candidate cells that have registered owners and no charger, by Spearman rank correlation and by overlap of the top 50. A stylised deployment simulation then runs each model as a siting rule for ten rounds of 15 sites, over all electrified cells with at least 240 kVA of headroom. The simulation needs a ground truth; one realisation is drawn from each cell's posterior and held fixed, so that neither rule knows it exactly. The observed record is regenerated each round: energy at a served cell equals a yield factor times its own true demand plus half the true demand of unserved cells within 12 km whose nearest served cell it is. This spillover term encodes the mobility of drivers; it is what makes the loop close. Rule A retrains Model A on the regenerated record each round and builds where it predicts most energy. Rule B builds where the latent-demand posterior mean is highest and does not retrain, because it does not use the record. Outcomes are the between-regency Gini of demand coverage, the share of latent demand covered in low-income regencies, and the mean distance of new sites to the nearest existing one.

4. Results

4.1 The models disagree about the next fifty sites

Figure 2. (a) Predicted energy from the observed-data model against posterior mean latent demand, for the 132 candidate cells; colour marks membership of each model's top 50. (b) Relative width of the 90 per cent posterior interval by cell status.

Figure 2(a) shows the core empirical result. Across candidate cells the two rankings correlate at ρ = 0.30, and only 26 of the 50 cells each model would build first are common to both. The disagreement is not random. Model A's exclusive picks lie, on average, 6.7 km from an existing charger; Model B's lie 5.8 km away but in cells with more registered owners. Model A is recommending cells that resemble served cells, dense grid, metropolitan coordinates, whether or not anyone there has bought an EV; Model B is recommending cells where people have bought EVs. Figure 4 maps the disagreement: Model A's exclusive picks ring the Jakarta commuter belt, Model B's include the Bandung basin and Sukabumi.

4.2 Uncertainty is largest where nothing has been observed

Figure 2(b) reports the relative width of the posterior interval. For served cells the median is 2.5; for cells with owners but no charger 2.2; for the 1057 cells with neither, 5.3, which is simply the width of the regency prior. The point is not that unserved cells with owners are more uncertain than served ones; on this measure they are slightly less so, because the register is observed everywhere. The point is that the majority of the province, the cells with no charger and no registered owner, receives from Model A a confident point prediction and from Model B an interval more than five times its mean. A transaction-trained model does not know that it does not know; a hierarchical model does, and says so in the cells where a wrong confident answer would matter most.

4.3 The loop closes

Figure 3. Ten rounds of 15 new sites under Rule A (retrain on the observed record) and Rule B (latent-demand posterior). (a) Between-regency Gini of demand coverage; (b) share of latent demand covered in low-income regencies; (c) mean distance of each round's new sites to the nearest existing site.

Figure 3 shows what happens when each model is allowed to drive deployment. Both rules start from the current network, with 74 per cent of latent demand covered and a between-regency Gini of 0.38. Rule B reaches 98 per cent coverage and a Gini of 0.15 after 150 sites; Rule A reaches 95 per cent and 0.27. The difference is concentrated where it matters. In low-income regencies, Rule B lifts coverage from 73 to 93 per cent; Rule A leaves it at 73 per cent through its first 45 sites and reaches only 81 per cent after 150. Panel (c) shows the mechanism: Rule A's first rounds are placed closer to existing sites than Rule B's, because spillover from unserved neighbours has been credited to those sites and the retrained model reads the credit as local demand. The loop is not dramatic in any single round. It is a steady bias that compounds, exactly as Ensign et al. (2018) predict, and it is invisible from inside the model, whose retrained fit improves each round as the record it created grows.

Figure 4. Candidate cells in each model's top 50. Cells chosen by both (blue), by the observed-data model only (red) and by the latent-demand model only (teal). Grey dots are existing sites.

5. Discussion

5.1 Sparsity is an artefact of allocation, not a property of the city

The siting literature's instinct is to treat the empty cells in Figure 1 as a data gap: cities without usage records need better proxies. This chapter's evidence points the other way. The empty cells are empty because the utility did not build there, and the utility did not build there, in part, because earlier decisions had produced no evidence that it should. Sparsity is the shadow of allocation. Treating it as missing-at-random noise, and smoothing it away with covariates that themselves encode the geography of investment, launders a distributive decision into an objective-looking forecast. Selbst et al. (2019) call this the framing trap: solving a sociotechnical problem as if it were a technical one and thereby importing the social structure into the solution. In charging deployment the trap has a map, and Figure 4 is it.

5.2 Design implications for planning support systems

Three implications follow for anyone building a siting model in a sparse network. First, separate exposure from observation. Any signal generated by the population rather than by the infrastructure, vehicle registrations, tariff applications, parking permits, can serve as exposure; the transaction log cannot. Second, pool. Hierarchical estimation with shrinkage towards regional means is standard in disease mapping and almost absent from infrastructure siting; it costs a few lines of code and produces the one thing a sparse-data model most needs, honest uncertainty. Third, publish the uncertainty. A planning support system that returns a ranked list of cells has hidden its own blind spot; one that returns a ranked list with intervals lets a planner see that the top of the list in an unserved regency is a guess and the top of the list in Bekasi is not. Geertman and Stillwell (2020) argue that PSS adoption depends on models that support argument rather than replace it; interval-bearing recommendations are what argument needs.

5.3 The politics of the prior

Partial pooling is not neutral either. Model B's regency hyperparameters encode an assumption that cells within a regency resemble one another, and its shrinkage weight encodes how much to trust a regency's own record against the province's. These are choices, and they have distributive content: a stronger prior lifts unserved regencies further. The chapter does not claim that Model B is right. It claims that Model B's assumptions are visible, in three parameters, whereas Model A's assumption that the future resembles the record is invisible, in five hundred trees. A model whose bias can be seen can be argued with. The argument for hierarchical latent-demand estimation in sparse networks is not that it removes politics from siting but that it puts the politics where a planner can find it.

5.4 Limitations

The simulation is stylised. Its ground truth is a single posterior draw, its spillover rule is a fixed fraction within a fixed radius, and it holds demand constant over ten rounds while a real network would see adoption respond to deployment; the results should be read as a demonstration of mechanism, not a forecast. Transformer count is an imperfect exposure measure that over-weights industrial areas. Registered home-charging customers under-represent households in multi-unit housing without off-street parking, so latent demand in dense urban cores is understated; the same limitation affects any register-based proxy and is the subject of the companion chapter on perceived quality. Model A is one observed-data model; a gradient-boosted or spatially cross-validated alternative would change the numbers but, by construction, not the direction, because no model can learn from transactions that were never generated.

6. Conclusion

A siting model trained on where charging happens will recommend more of where charging happens. In a network built ahead of demand that is not a forecast but a repetition, and the chapter has measured how much of one: two models on identical territory agree on half of their first fifty sites, and over ten rounds of deployment the transaction-trained rule leaves a fifth of latent demand in low-income regencies unserved while the latent-demand rule leaves a fifteenth. The remedy is not more data, which cannot exist until the infrastructure does. It is an inferential design that separates the population's signal from the infrastructure's record, borrows strength across space in proportion to ignorance, and reports what it does not know. For the wider debate about AI in cities, West Java offers a concrete instance of a claim usually made in the abstract: that urban AI reproduces the geography of past investment unless it is explicitly designed not to, and that the design choices which prevent it are neither exotic nor expensive.

papers.abstract: In a network built ahead of demand, the transaction record a siting model learns from is not a sample of demand but a record of previous allocation decisions. This chapter shows, with operator data from West Java, Indonesia, that the conventional data-driven siting pipeline contains a feedback loop with distributive consequences. Observed transactions exist in only 174 of 1295 five-kilometre cells; 132 cells hold 908 registered EV owners and no charger. We compare two models on the same territory: a random forest fitted to observed transactions using grid and geographic covariates, and a Gamma–Poisson hierarchical model of latent demand that partially pools an exposure signal independent of charger placement, 3,687 households registered for the home-charging tariff. The models agree only weakly on where to build next (Spearman ρ = 0.30; 26 of the top 50 cells in common), and posterior uncertainty is widest exactly where no infrastructure and no observation exist. A deployment simulation shows why the difference compounds: demand from unserved cells is credited to the nearest served site, and a model retrained on that record keeps recommending densification. After ten rounds the observed-data rule leaves 19 per cent of latent demand in low-income regencies unserved against 7 per cent for the latent-demand rule. Sparsity is an artefact of an earlier distributive choice; treating missing data as missing demand launders that choice into a forecast. The chapter proposes an inferential design that separates exposure from observation and reports uncertainty as a first-class output of any planning support system.

From Access to Use: Large Language Models as a Participation Surface for Charging Infrastructure, and the Class Filter They Inherit

Qashtalani Haramaini — Monash University Indonesia (RACE for 2030 Program) / PT PLN (Persero) UID Jawa Barat, Indonesia — qashtalani.haramaini@monash.edu (corresponding and presenting author) · Alyas Widita — Monash University Indonesia — alyas.widita@monash.edu · Liz Taylor — Monash University, Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture (MADA), Australia — liz.taylor@monash.edu

CUPUM 2027 — Future Cities in the Era of AI · Book chapter (full manuscript draft)

Abstract

Counting chargers measures presence, not usability. Where no formal participation channel exists, the only systematic record of how charging is experienced is user-generated review text; this chapter treats it as a participation surface and asks what it reveals and whom it fails to hear. Using aspect-based sentiment analysis with a large language model, we score 584 charging locations in and around West Java, Indonesia, on seven service aspects and aggregate them into a Station Quality Index (SQI). Reliability and availability dominate perceived quality, and the seven aspects explain 63 per cent of SQI variance. Joining SQI to population-weighted concentration indices across 19 cities and regencies ranked by Human Development Index, we find that hardware is distributed almost neutrally (CI = +0.06) while use is strongly pro-rich (energy per capita CI = +0.34; EV ownership CI = +0.45), and that perceived quality is flat across the income gradient (CI = -0.02). The reliability problem is network-wide, not peripheral. But the surface that reports this is skewed: PLN sites in the highest-HDI tercile attract 8.3 reviews each, those in the lowest 4.0, and only 38 per cent of low-HDI sites have enough reviews to score. LLM-mediated feedback reproduces a class filter while wearing the appearance of public voice. We propose a two-dimensional equity framework, access and experience, and a coverage audit as the condition for using scraped sentiment in planning.

Keywords: aspect-based sentiment analysis; large language models; vertical equity; public participation; user-generated content; electric vehicle charging

1. Introduction

The equity of public EV charging is almost always assessed by counting. Chargers per capita, chargers per square kilometre, Gini coefficients of chargers across districts, distance from each household to the nearest charger: the metrics differ but the object is the same, the presence of hardware in space (Hsu and Fingerman, 2021; Lou et al., 2024; Falchetta and Noussan, 2021). Presence is necessary. It is not sufficient. A charger that has been offline for a month, that is permanently occupied by a vehicle that is not charging, that delivers 22 kW when its sign says 60, or whose payment application rejects every card, is counted as access by every one of these metrics and experienced as none by every driver who tries it. The transport-justice literature has long insisted that accessibility is about what people can actually do, not what exists near them (Martens, 2017; Pereira et al., 2017). Charging research has been slow to take the point.

Part of the reason is data. Usability is not in any asset register. Where regulators require operators to report uptime, as in California and under the EU's Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation, some of it can be reconstructed; in most of the world nothing of the kind exists. Indonesia has no uptime reporting, no consultation requirement for charging deployment and no service-quality regulator with a public complaints record. The only systematic account of how charging is experienced is what drivers write about it on mapping platforms, and until recently that account was too unstructured to use.

Large language models change this. Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) can read thousands of free-text reviews and code each on a fixed set of service dimensions with a consistency no human panel could sustain, and Asensio et al. (2020) have shown, at national scale in the United States, that platform reviews classified by machine learning reveal reliability failures invisible to operators' own data. This chapter applies that approach to West Java and joins it to distributive-equity analysis, producing what we believe is the first two-dimensional equity assessment of a charging network in the Global South: how much hardware people have, and how well the hardware they have works for them.

The chapter is deliberately in two halves. The first treats review text as a participation surface and reports what it shows: which aspects drive experienced quality, and whether quality follows the same income gradient that use does. The second turns the method on itself and asks whom the surface hears. Reviews are written by people who own an EV, a smartphone and a platform account, and who choose to write. In Indonesia that is an affluent, digitally fluent minority, and the chapter shows that it is also a spatially skewed one. As generative models increasingly mediate how residents interact with government, the temptation to treat scraped sentiment as consultation will grow. The second half is a measured argument for resisting it.

2. Background

2.1 Horizontal and vertical equity in charging

Horizontal equity asks whether like areas are treated alike; vertical equity asks whether disadvantaged groups are treated better, worse or the same (Pereira et al., 2017). Charging-equity research has been almost entirely horizontal, using Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients of chargers across spatial units (Delbosc and Currie, 2011, in the transit tradition), or regression of charger presence on neighbourhood income and ethnicity (Hsu and Fingerman, 2021; Roy and Law, 2022). Vertical equity requires ranking areas by socio-economic status and asking whether provision concentrates at the top or the bottom. The concentration index of health economics does exactly this (Wagstaff et al., 1991; O'Donnell et al., 2008): the population-weighted covariance between a measure and the fractional socio-economic rank, scaled so that +1 means the measure is held entirely by the richest, −1 by the poorest, and 0 is neutral. It has rarely been applied to charging, and never, to our knowledge, to a measure of experienced quality.

2.2 Perceived environmental quality and PPGIS

Planning has a long tradition of treating perceived quality as data. Kyttä and colleagues' softGIS work showed that residents' located experiences of their environment could be collected at scale and used to reveal quality gradients that administrative data missed (Kyttä et al., 2011; Kyttä et al., 2013), and public-participation GIS has developed methods for eliciting such data deliberately (Brown and Kyttä, 2014). The distinctive feature of platform reviews is that they are not elicited. They are volunteered, by whoever chooses to volunteer, and the literature on volunteered geographic information has been clear since Haklay (2013) that this democratises the appearance of participation more than the substance: contributors are disproportionately urban, male, affluent and technically fluent (Hecht and Stephens, 2014). Ilieva and McPhearson (2018) argue that social-media data can nonetheless support urban sustainability research if their biases are measured rather than assumed away. That is the stance taken here.

2.3 Machine reading of infrastructure experience

Asensio et al. (2020) classified 127,000 reviews of US charging stations with a convolutional network and found that reliability complaints were concentrated at publicly funded sites; Ha et al. (2021) extended the approach with transformer models for topic classification. Both treat the review corpus as a sensor of infrastructure performance. Neither joins it to distributive equity, and neither examines the corpus's own coverage. The methodological contribution of this chapter is that join, and the critical contribution is the coverage audit.

3. Data and methods

3.1 The review corpus and the Station Quality Index

Public reviews were collected for 894 charging locations in West Java and the adjacent Jakarta metropolitan area, of which 584 had sufficient review volume to be scored (244 in West Java, 340 outside). Each review was passed to a large language model with a fixed prompt that codes seven service aspects on a −1/0/+1 scale, with fractional values where a location's reviews disagree: reliability (does the charger work), availability (is it free when needed), delivered power (does it charge at the advertised rate), payment, facilities, staff service and connector compatibility. Aspect codes were aggregated per location and combined with the Bayesian-shrunk star rating into a Station Quality Index (SQI) on a 0–100 scale; a confidence flag records review volume. The scored set spans seven operators, with PLN accounting for 150 locations and independent operators for the remainder.

3.2 What drives perceived quality

Two analyses identify the aspects that determine SQI. The first compares mean SQI between locations where an aspect is coded positive and locations where it is coded negative; the difference is the aspect's impact. The second is an ordinary-least-squares regression of SQI on the seven aspect codes with unmentioned aspects set to zero, which estimates each aspect's contribution holding the others constant.

3.3 Distributive measures

Population, Human Development Index (HDI) and income tier for 19 city and regency groups were taken from Statistics Indonesia and the provincial Klassen typology; PLN's Master SPKLU register (636 units at 348 sites) and the March 2026 transaction log (101,020 sessions) supplied units per 100,000 residents and energy per capita; the home-charging customer register supplied EV owners per 100,000. Four measures were computed for each group: chargers per 100,000, energy per capita, EV owners per 100,000 and mean SQI of scored locations. For each, a population-weighted concentration index against HDI rank was calculated following Wagstaff et al. (1991), together with the corresponding concentration curve. Horizontal-equity Gini coefficients of units and of energy against population were also computed.

3.4 Coverage audit

To measure whom the review surface hears, scored locations and total review counts were tallied per city and regency and divided by the number of PLN sites in the Master register, giving scored locations per site and reviews per site. Groups were split into HDI terciles. Because independent operators also appear in the review corpus, the ratio can exceed one; it is a measure of review density relative to the public network, not a coverage rate.

4. Results

4.1 The shape of experienced quality

Figure 1. (a) Distribution of the Station Quality Index across 584 scored locations. (b) Net aspect sentiment across all reviews; n is the number of locations at which the aspect was mentioned.

Figure 1(a) shows a bimodal network. The median SQI is 77 and 271 locations score 80 or above, but 100 score below 40: a network in which most stations work well and a large minority are, by their users' account, barely functional. Figure 1(b) shows what users talk about. Facilities and staff service are praised; reliability is neutral on balance; availability, payment and delivered power are net negative, with delivered power the most negative aspect at -0.30. Reviewers are not complaining about amenities. They are complaining that the charger did not work, was occupied, would not take their money or did not deliver what its label promised.

Table 1 ranks the aspects by impact. Reliability and availability are decisive: a location praised for reliability scores 84 on average and one criticised for it 45, a gap of 38 points; availability's gap is 34. Holding the other aspects constant, availability contributes 14 points and reliability 13, payment 9 and delivered power 8; facilities, the most praised aspect, contributes 6, and connectors are not significant. The seven aspects explain 63 per cent of the variance in SQI. The implication for a coverage-first roll-out is direct: the marginal review point is bought by keeping existing chargers working and free, not by adding a café.

4.2 Hardware is neutral, use is pro-rich, quality is flat

Figure 2. (a) Concentration curves against HDI rank for four measures across 19 city and regency groups, with concentration indices. (b) Mean SQI of scored locations against HDI; bubble size is population, colour is provincial income tier.

Figure 2(a) reports the vertical-equity result. Chargers per 100,000 residents are distributed almost neutrally across the HDI gradient (CI = +0.06): the public network, dominated by PLN office sites in every regency, has put hardware roughly where people are. Use is another matter. Energy per capita concentrates strongly among more affluent areas (CI = +0.34) and EV ownership more strongly still (CI = +0.45). The horizontal Gini tells the same story: units against population 0.19, energy against population 0.45. The network is equal in presence and unequal in use, because the cars are unequal.

The chapter's central hypothesis was that a quality gradient would sit on top of this use gradient: that less advantaged areas would receive not only fewer users but worse-performing chargers, so that deprivation compounds. The data do not support it. The concentration index of SQI is -0.02, indistinguishable from zero, and Figure 2(b) shows no relationship between a regency's HDI and the quality its stations receive (r = -0.18, n = 18). Among West Java's scored locations, mean SQI is 72 in low-income regencies, 68 in medium and 71 in high. Sumedang, at 40, is an outlier on a single location. The reliability and availability problems that dominate Table 1 are not a peripheral problem; they are a network problem, as likely to be reported in Bekasi as in Garut.

Figure 3. The 584 review-scored locations coloured by SQI and sized by review count, over the PLN Master site register (grey). Low-SQI locations are scattered through the Jakarta belt and Greater Bandung rather than confined to the periphery.

Figure 3 makes the point spatially. Red, low-SQI locations sit inside the Jakarta commuter belt and the Bandung basin among green ones; the periphery has few scored locations of either colour. That last observation is the pivot to the second half of the chapter.

4.3 Whom the surface hears

Figure 4. Review density relative to the public network. (a) Reviews per PLN site by HDI tercile of the city or regency. (b) Reviews per PLN site by city and regency against HDI; bubble size is population, colour is income tier.

Figure 4 is the coverage audit. PLN sites in the highest-HDI tercile of cities and regencies attract 8.3 reviews each; sites in the middle tercile 5.5; sites in the lowest 4.0. Scored locations per PLN site are 0.82, 0.77 and 0.38 respectively: in the poorest third of the province fewer than two in five public sites generate enough reviews to be assessed at all. Bekasi, the richest large regency, produces 18 reviews per site; Sumedang produces 0.7 and Pangandaran none. The surface is loudest where the cars are.

This reframes the flat quality gradient of Section 4.2. It is a real finding, but it is measured on 36 scored locations in the low-HDI tercile against 143 in the high tercile, and the low-tercile locations that reach the scoring threshold are, by construction, the ones that attract enough traffic to be reviewed. If the worst charger in a poor regency is one nobody uses because it has never worked, it has no reviews, no SQI and no place in Figure 2. The participation surface cannot see the failure it would most need to report.

5. Discussion

5.1 A two-dimensional equity framework

The results support separating charging equity into two dimensions that behave differently. Access, measured by hardware per capita, is close to neutral in West Java; use, measured by energy and ownership, is strongly pro-rich; experienced quality, measured by review sentiment, shows no gradient. A one-dimensional assessment based on counting would conclude that the network is equitable. A one-dimensional assessment based on energy would conclude that it is not. Both are right about their dimension and wrong about the network. The framework proposed here reports access and experience side by side, because a planning response differs by quadrant: where access is low, build; where access is adequate and experience poor, maintain; where both are adequate and use is low, the constraint is the car, not the charger, and charging policy cannot fix it.

5.2 What the machine can read and what it cannot

LLM-based ABSA is a real advance. It converts an unstructured corpus into a consistent, aspect-level measure of infrastructure performance that no operator in Indonesia currently produces and no regulator requires, and it does so at a marginal cost close to zero. Table 1 is actionable: it tells a utility that its reputation is made by reliability and availability, and that the most-praised aspect, facilities, buys the least. The method should be used. But Figure 4 shows the condition under which it should be used. The corpus is a census of the people who already have EVs, smartphones and accounts, weighted by their propensity to write, and its spatial distribution follows theirs. Haklay's (2013) warning about the delusion of democratisation applies with full force: the platform looks like a public and is a customer base. Treating its sentiment as consultation would let the loudest third of the province set the maintenance priorities of the whole.

5.3 Implications for participation in the era of AI

CUPUM's call notes that large language models increasingly mediate how residents interact with government. This chapter offers a concrete case of what that mediation does when it is passive rather than elicited. Arnstein's (1969) ladder distinguished participation from its appearance; scraped sentiment sits on the lower rungs, informing without conferring any power, and the coverage audit shows that even the informing is partial. Three practices follow. First, publish the coverage audit alongside any sentiment-derived indicator, so that the population it represents is visible. Second, treat gaps in the surface as findings, not as missing data: a public site with no reviews in a low-income regency is a site to inspect, not a site to drop from the sample. Third, use the machine-read corpus to target elicited participation, in the softGIS tradition (Kyttä et al., 2013; Brown and Kyttä, 2014), at precisely the places and populations it cannot hear. The model is a good listener with a bad microphone; the fix is the microphone.

5.4 Limitations

The review corpus is drawn from a single mapping platform and its threshold for scoring excludes low-traffic locations by design. Aspect coding by an LLM was validated on a sample but not against an independent human panel at scale. The socio-economic analysis uses 19 city and regency groups, a coarse spatial unit that hides within-regency inequality, and HDI as a single status ranking. PLN-only site counts in the denominator of the coverage audit understate the private network in affluent areas, which would make the class skew larger, not smaller. The flat quality gradient is a null result on limited low-HDI data and should be read as absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence.

6. Conclusion

Counting chargers measures presence; reading reviews measures experience; neither alone measures equity. In West Java the hardware is spread almost neutrally, the use is strongly pro-rich, and the experienced quality, where it can be measured, is the same poor-to-good mixture everywhere, dominated by whether the charger works and is free. That is worth knowing and could not have been known without a machine that reads. But the machine reads a corpus that the affluent write, at twice the density, and the poorest third of the province's public sites are mostly silent within it. A two-dimensional equity framework that reports access and experience together, and a coverage audit that reports who was heard, are the minimum conditions under which LLM-derived sentiment can inform infrastructure planning without becoming one more way in which those who already have the most also have the loudest say.

PAPER 3 — DRAFT

Working title: Charging without selling electricity: a parking-and-service fee architecture for peer-to-peer EV charging under a single-buyer electricity regime — evidence from West Java, Indonesia

Target journal (primary): Energy Policy (Elsevier, Q1) Alternatives: Energy Research & Social Science (Q1) · Utilities Policy (Q2) · Transport Policy (Q1)

Draft note: every figure in this manuscript is produced by papers/p2p/prepare.py from the raw project datasets (PLN UID West Java transaction detail and home-charging application register, March–June 2026). Re-run that script and the numbers here can be reproduced line by line. Citations and legal-clause references marked [VERIFY] are placeholders that must be checked against the primary texts before submission.

Structured abstract (≈300 words)

Context. Peer-to-peer (P2P) charging — a household renting out its private wallbox to another driver — is the cheapest way to add EV charging capacity, because the asset is already built. In most markets the transaction is straightforward: the host sells kilowatt-hours. In Indonesia it is not. Supplying electricity to the public is a licensed activity; an individual customer reselling kWh has no licence to do it. The literature on P2P charging assumes away exactly the constraint that binds in the largest EV market of Southeast Asia.

Objective. We ask whether a P2P charging market can be built without the sale of energy, and what such a market does to prices, host income, platform economics, utility revenue, network peak load, and spatial equity.

Data & methods. We use 100,782 metered public-charging sessions (2.26 GWh, Rp 5.89 bn, March 2026) across 329 public stations in West Java, and the register of 3,694 PLN home-charging connection applications (2,181 completed) to June 2026, geocoded to 695 villages. We derive a fee architecture in which the driver pays a parking rate (Rp/hour) plus a flat service fee (Rp/session) and no kWh changes hands; the energy remains a residential sale from the utility to the host. We solve the architecture analytically for its feasible price band, break-even dwell time and surplus split, then quantify a four-sided financial model (host, driver, platform, utility), the load-shift effect, and Gini/Lorenz equity outcomes.

Results. (i) The entire business lives inside a band of Rp 8,328–16,981 per hour at 7 kW, whose two edges are set by tariffs the host does not control. (ii) A time-based fee is floored in Rp/kWh terms and therefore only beats public charging above a break-even dwell of 1.44 hours (9.3 kWh) — the architecture is structurally an overnight product and structurally unsuited to top-ups. (iii) Because host revenue accrues per hour rather than per kWh, the host's incentive is to maximise occupancy, not throughput — the legal constraint accidentally aligns private incentive with system benefit. (iv) 2,181 already-installed home chargers hold 2.96 GWh/month of idle overnight capacity, 1.31× the entire public network's output, equivalent to 431 public fast- charging sites and about Rp 518 bn of avoided capital. (v) 64.8 % of recorded public sessions (56.8 % of energy) are technically substitutable. (vi) The utility gains: at 20 % substitution, avoided capital and O&M of Rp 8.08 bn/year exceed revenue dilution of Rp 3.66 bn/year. (vii) But hosts are more spatially concentrated than the public network they would supplement (Gini 0.599 vs 0.264 against population; ρ = 0.73 with existing demand). P2P is an efficiency instrument, not an equity instrument.

Implications. We derive a five-step regulatory ladder that makes the architecture lawful and then makes it fair, centred on a dedicated host-meter tariff class and a mandatory disclosure of effective Rp/kWh at booking.

Keywords: peer-to-peer charging; EV charging; electricity market regulation; two-part tariff; platform design; energy justice; Indonesia

1. Introduction

The cheapest charge point is the one already installed. By June 2026 the utility's West Java distribution region had processed 3,694 applications for dedicated home-charging connections and completed 2,181 of them, spread across 231 sub-districts and 695 villages. Each is a 7,700 VA single-phase service feeding a ~7 kW wallbox that, as Section 5.2 shows, sits unused about 87 % of the nights it could be working. In the same province the public network — 329 stations that recorded a transaction in March 2026 — sold 2.26 GWh at an all-in Rp 2,608/kWh.

The arithmetic invites an obvious question. If idle household chargers could be rented to drivers who have none, the province would add charging capacity at nearly zero marginal capital cost, using assets that have already been paid for and connections that have already been engineered. This is the peer-to-peer (P2P) proposition, and internationally it is not exotic: platforms in the UK, the Netherlands and the United States operate host-listed home chargers as a straightforward marketplace. [VERIFY: Co Charger; Joosup; EVmatch; Plugshare Home]

What makes Indonesia different is that the obvious form of the transaction is closed. Supplying electricity to the public is a licensed activity under Law 30/2009 on Electricity; selling surplus electricity for public use without government approval carries criminal liability (Art. 49(3): up to two years and Rp 2 bn, narrowed by the Job Creation Law to cases producing harm). [VERIFY: exact clause numbering after UU 6/2023] Public charging stations (SPKLU) are classified under business code KBLI 35114 — sale of electric power — a high-risk activity requiring a business identification number and an electricity supply business licence, with the price to the vehicle owner set from the special-service tariff class at a multiplier of at most 1.5. [VERIFY: Permen ESDM 1/2023, Arts. 10, 15 and the tariff annex] A household with a residential connection holds none of this. It cannot lawfully resell the kilowatt-hours it buys.

Almost the entire P2P charging literature is written for jurisdictions where that constraint does not exist, and therefore treats the design problem as one of matching, pricing and trust. [VERIFY: P2P charging platform literature] The Indonesian case forces a prior question: can the market be built at all if the thing being traded cannot be the energy?

This paper answers yes, and shows that the answer is not merely a workaround. Re-basing the transaction from energy to time and space — a parking rate plus a service fee, with the kWh remaining a residential sale from the utility to the host — changes the economics in ways that are mostly, and surprisingly, favourable to the electricity system. We set out the architecture, solve it, quantify it against a full month of metered demand and a complete host register, and derive the policy sequence that would make it lawful and then make it fair.

Contributions.

  1. A formal fee architecture for P2P charging under a licensing regime that forbids energy resale,

with closed-form expressions for its feasible price band and break-even dwell time.

  1. The proposition — derived, then quantified — that the fee base determines the load shape:

per-kWh pricing rewards throughput and therefore peak-hour turnover; per-hour pricing rewards occupancy and therefore overnight charging.

  1. A four-sided financial model (host, driver, platform, utility) estimated on real transactions

rather than survey intentions, including the revenue dilution the utility must absorb.

  1. The first measurement, to our knowledge, of the idle overnight capacity already installed in a

developing-country home-charging fleet, benchmarked against the public network it could relieve.

  1. An equity result that cuts against the usual advocacy: P2P supply is more spatially concentrated

than the public network, and will widen access gaps unless deliberately steered.

2. The constraint, taken seriously

2.1 What is actually forbidden

Three legal facts define the design space. [VERIFY: all three against primary texts]

FactInstrumentConsequence for P2P
Supplying electricity to the public is a licensed activity; unlicensed sale of surplus power is prohibited and criminally sanctionedUU 30/2009 Art. 49(3), as amended by UU 6/2023A household cannot price its wallbox in Rp/kWh
Public charging (SPKLU) is business code KBLI 35114 sale of electric power, high risk, requiring NIB + electricity supply licencePermen ESDM 1/2023 Arts. 10 & 15; PP 5/2021 Art. 15(1)Becoming a licensed operator is not proportionate for a single 7 kW socket
The SPKLU price to the vehicle owner derives from the special-service tariff class with multiplier N ≤ 1.5Permen ESDM 1/2023 tariff provisionsThe public price is administratively set, not competed — so it is a stable ceiling to price against

The prohibition is on selling energy, not on being paid. A hotel that charges for parking and offers a socket, a mall that bundles charging into a validated parking ticket, and an office that recovers costs through a facilities fee are all doing something the law contemplates. The architecture below simply makes that structure explicit, priced, and bookable.

2.2 Two architectures

Model A — the Airbnb transposition (per-kWh). The host lists a price \(p_h\) in Rp/kWh; the platform takes a commission \(\theta\); the host's electricity cost is the residential tariff. This is the international norm and the economically cleanest form. In Indonesia today it is the one thing that cannot be done.

Model B — parking and service (per-hour + per-session). The driver books a bay for a period. The driver pays a parking rate \(r\) (Rp/hour) to the host and a flat service fee \(F\) (Rp/session) to the platform. No kilowatt-hours are bought or sold at any point. The energy flowing through the host's meter remains a residential sale from the utility to the host, at the host's own tariff, exactly as it would be if the host's own car were plugged in.

The rest of the paper treats Model B as the deployable design and Model A as the benchmark and the post-reform target state.

2.3 Solving Model B

Let \(P\) be the connection's usable AC power (kW), \(\eta\) the AC charging efficiency, \(t\) the booked dwell (hours), \(p_s\) the all-in public price (Rp/kWh) and \(p_0\) the host's own tariff.

Two energy quantities must be kept apart, and conflating them is the most common error in back-of-envelope P2P models:

  • Metered energy \(E_m = P\,t\) — what the host's meter records and what the host pays for.
  • Battery energy \(E_b = P\,t\,\eta\) — what the driver receives and values.

The driver's cost per useful kWh is therefore

$$c(t)\;=\;\frac{F + r\,t}{P\,t\,\eta}\;=\;\underbrace{\frac{F}{P\,\eta\,t}}_{\text{decays with dwell}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{r}{P\,\eta}}_{\text{hard floor}}$$

Three properties follow immediately.

(P1) A price floor the driver can never get below. As \(t \to \infty\), \(c \to r/(P\eta)\). The parking rate divided by delivered power is a hard floor in Rp/kWh. For the architecture ever to beat public charging, \(r < P\,\eta\,p_s\).

(P2) A break-even dwell. Setting \(c(t^\*) = p_s\),

$$t^\* \;=\; \frac{F}{P\,\eta\,p_s - r}$$

Below \(t^\\) the P2P session is more* expensive than the public network. The architecture is structurally hostile to short top-ups and structurally suited to long dwell.

(P3) A feasible band with two exogenous edges. The host must not subsidise the guest's energy, so \(r > P\,p_0\); the driver must be better off, so \(r < P\,\eta\,p_s\). Hence

$$P\,p_0 \;<\; r \;<\; P\,\eta\,p_s$$

Both edges are set by administratively determined tariffs. The entire commercial design space of P2P charging in Indonesia is a band whose width neither the host, the driver nor the platform can influence.

2.4 The fee base determines the load shape

This is the paper's central proposition, and it is a consequence of the algebra rather than of the data.

Under Model A the host's revenue is \(R_A = (1-\theta)\,p_h\,P\,\eta\,t\): proportional to power. A rational host upgrades the connection, installs a faster wallbox, and prefers many short high-power sessions — precisely the behaviour that stacks new load onto the low-voltage network and, because demand for charging is highest in the evening, onto the system peak.

Under Model B the host's revenue is \(R_B = r\,t\): independent of power. The host is indifferent to how fast the guest charges and cares only that the bay is occupied. The rational host therefore seeks long, uninterrupted bookings — overnight — and has no incentive whatsoever to increase connected power.

The regulatory constraint, in other words, does not merely permit a second-best market. It removes the private incentive to add peak-coincident household capacity, and replaces it with an incentive to fill the trough. Section 5.6 quantifies the effect.

Household-level records are aggregated and pseudonymised; no individual applicant is identifiable. Coordinates are used only to compute distances to public stations and counts per administrative unit.

3.1 Operationalising "substitutable"

A recorded public session is counted as P2P-substitutable when all three hold:

  1. Not corridor charging. Sessions at toll-road rest areas are excluded. There the reason for

stopping is DC speed on an intercity trip; a 7 kW socket at someone's house is not a substitute.

  1. A host exists in the neighbourhood. The station lies within 3 km of at least one completed

home-charging installation. This is a proxy for matchability, not a claim about any individual driver's origin, and it is deliberately generous: results at 1, 2, 5 and 10 km are reported.

  1. The energy fits one night. Session energy ≤ 45.6 kWh, the amount a 7 kW AC connection

delivers to a battery across a seven-hour window at \(\eta = 0.93\).

This is an upper bound on geographic matchability, not a demand forecast. It says how much of the recorded demand could physically have been served by a neighbourhood wallbox, and nothing about willingness on either side.

4. Method

All quantities are produced by papers/p2p/prepare.py, in seven blocks: (A) market baseline; (B) host supply and idle capacity; (C) substitutable demand; (D) fee architecture, feasible band and power-risk sensitivity; (E) four-sided financials; (F) network load shift; (G) equity.

Parameters and their provenance. \(p_s = 2{,}608.39\) Rp/kWh and its decomposition are computed from the transactions themselves, not assumed. \(p_0 = 1{,}699.53\) Rp/kWh is the residential tariff for ≥3,500 VA [VERIFY]; the night rate \(p_0^{n} = 1{,}189.67\) applies the utility's 30 % home-charging discount for 22:00–05:00 [VERIFY: promotional period 1 Jul 2025 – 30 Jun 2026]. \(P = 7.0\) kW reflects the 7,700 VA single-phase connection that 3,553 of 3,694 applicants took. \(\eta = 0.93\) follows the project's charging model. Capital benchmarks — Rp 1.2 bn per public DC site, Rp 96 m/year site O&M, Rp 18 m per installed home wallbox, 10-year life — are indicative and flagged [VERIFY]; the utility results in Section 5.5 are reported as sensitivities against them.

Equity. Gini coefficients and Lorenz curves are computed against population for three quantities per city/regency: public stations, public energy consumed, and home-charging hosts. Spearman rank correlations relate host counts to existing demand and existing supply.

5. Results

5.1 The gap the whole model has to live in

March 2026 public charging in West Java cost an all-in Rp 2,608.39/kWh: an energy component of Rp 2,466.75 plus a municipal public-lighting levy averaging Rp 141.62, which varies from 5 % to 10 % by municipality and makes the same kilowatt-hour cost Rp 2,590 in one regency and Rp 2,713 in another. Mean session size was 22.42 kWh over 53.9 minutes (medians 19.82 kWh, 40.9 minutes).

Against a residential tariff of Rp 1,699.53, the gross surplus available to any P2P arrangement is Rp 908.86/kWh; against the discounted night rate of Rp 1,189.67 it is Rp 1,418.72/kWh. That surplus is the only thing there is to divide among four parties.

Two things follow. First, the night discount does not merely make charging cheaper; it widens the commercial band by 70 %, from Rp 5,084 to Rp 8,653 per hour. Second — and this is a fragility the business plan must confront — that discount is a promotion with an expiry date (1 July 2025 – 30 June 2026) [VERIFY], not a structural tariff. A P2P market built on it is built on an administrative decision that can lapse.

5.2 The capacity is already installed, and it is idle

A household driving 1,200 km/month at 0.17 kWh/km needs 204 kWh into the battery, or 219 kWh metered — 31.3 charger-hours per month, equivalent to 3.9 full nights out of thirty. Against a shareable window of eight hours per night, 86.9 % of the household charger's night capacity is unused.

The absolute magnitudes are small today — a province whose system peak is measured in gigawatts is not rescued by one megawatt. They matter for two reasons. First, they scale with the EV fleet while the network's capacity to absorb evening charging does not. Second, the shape of what P2P adds is different in kind: a public site concentrates 120 kW at one low-voltage connection, while the same energy served by hosts is spread over 17 separate 7 kW connections on 17 different service drops. Under Model B, as Section 2.4 established, the host has no revenue reason to increase that power. The architecture disperses load by construction.

5.7 The uncomfortable equity result

The advocacy case for P2P is that it reaches places a capital-intensive public rollout will not. Against the West Java data, it does not.

Home chargers are more unequally distributed than the public network they are supposed to supplement, and more unequally distributed than public consumption itself. Rank correlations confirm the mechanism: host counts correlate with existing public energy at ρ = 0.73 and with existing station counts at ρ = 0.71. Hosts appear where charging demand already is — the four largest host populations (Kab. Bogor 787, Kota Depok 663, Kota Bandung 462, Kota Bekasi 400) are the same places that already dominate public consumption. Kab. Pangandaran has no hosts at all; Kab. Ciamis has no public station.

The reason is structural rather than accidental. A home-charging connection requires home ownership or a landlord's consent, a garage or private frontage, and about Rp 18 m of capital. Those conditions are distributed like wealth, and wealth is distributed like the existing public network.

The conclusion follows and should not be softened: peer-to-peer charging is an efficiency instrument, not an equity instrument. It lowers the cost of serving demand where hosts already exist. Left to itself it deepens the core–periphery split that Paper 1 measured. If it is to serve equity, the steering must be deliberate and fiscal — Section 7.

There is, however, a real distributional gain hiding inside the aggregate. The customer for P2P is by definition a driver who cannot install a wallbox — an apartment resident, a renter, a household in dense kampung housing — and who therefore pays the full public price today. Table 7 puts that driver's saving at Rp 89,485/month. P2P transfers surplus from those with off-street parking to those without, within the districts where both live. It is progressive within places and regressive between them.

5.8 Who bears the power risk

Under a time-based fee, the effective price per kWh is inversely proportional to the power the car actually accepts. This risk does not exist under per-kWh pricing, and it falls entirely on the driver.

For the actual host fleet the exposure is modest — makes weighted by their share of the register give an effective AC power of 6.85 kW, and the spread across the top ten makes is only Rp 2,170–2,301/kWh — because the Indonesian market is dominated by 6.6–7 kW onboard chargers. But a driver whose vehicle accepts 3.3 kW pays 76 % more than the public network for the same booking and has no way to know it from the listing. Any competent implementation must therefore compute and display the expected effective Rp/kWh for the specific vehicle at the moment of booking, not the parking rate. We treat this as a consumer-protection requirement, not a product nicety (Section 7, step 4).

6. The Airbnb scheme, transposed

The user-facing product is an Airbnb for parking bays that happen to have a socket. Every Airbnb primitive maps, and the three that do not map are the ones that matter.
